According to BOLT2, messages can be sent in batches to be treated as a single logical update through the start_batch message, which among other fields carries the batch_size. According to the specifications, the size must be at most 20 and strictly greater than 1. While Eclair checked for the upper bound, it did not enforce the lower one.

Poinsot considered that effect most likely small but not worth working out rigorously.

title: Homeland Security Launches New Centre to Hit Crypto Scams, Cybercrime and Sextortion Networks
description: TRM Labs has been selected to supply the investigative technology for the new US government initiative targeting online scams and cybercrime.
fullContent:
The Homeland Security Task Force (HSTF) has launched a Threat Disruption Center to combat cryptocurrency fraud, cybercrime, online scams, and sextortion schemes targeting Americans. The new unit will operate within the HSTF’s National Coordination Center (NCC).

The main objective is to disrupt the flow of stolen money to foreign criminal networks by bringing law enforcement agencies and private-sector companies together to act on intelligence more quickly.

Disrupting Global Scam Networks

Co-led by the Department of Homeland Security and the Department of Justice, the NCC will bring together more than 30 federal agencies and over 440 state and local partners. The center will provide investigators with shared technology to assess victim complaints, trace criminal networks, and identify their infrastructure, while establishing a channel for coordination with companies that can intervene before further losses occur.

These interventions could include pausing suspicious payments, taking down malicious websites, as well as banning social media accounts used to target victims. Companies can take such action under their own terms of service, while law enforcement continues its investigations, prosecutions and court-authorised seizures.

The initiative comes as reported losses from cybercrime continue to rise. The FBI’s Internet Crime Complaint Center recorded $20.9 billion in victim losses in 2025. This excludes people who never report being scammed, so the actual figure could be much higher. The National Center for Missing & Exploited Children, meanwhile, received an average of 137 reports of financial sextortion involving minors each day that year.

HSTF said criminal networks increasingly rely on social media, web infrastructure, banking, payment services and crypto platforms to reach victims and move illicit proceeds. The Threat Disruption Center is intended to use those same points of contact to interrupt their operations.

TRM Labs Joins Forces

TRM Labs has been selected as the newly formed entity’s primary private-sector partner to provide the technology and operational support behind its investigations. The company will deploy Ardence, its super intelligence (SI) orchestration platform, as Threat Disruption Center’s main investigative tool, in addition to dedicated engineering and investigative teams.

The platform is designed to help investigators identify different parts of criminal networks, map their infrastructure, and establish the extent of their victim base. TRM will also support the coordination of intelligence between government agencies and participating companies to enable faster responses to suspected scams and the movement of stolen funds.

The post Homeland Security Launches New Centre to Hit Crypto Scams, Cybercrime and Sextortion Networks appeared first on CryptoPotato.

title: From MAGA stardom to a U-Haul: Lauren Boebert considers her own and GOP's losses
description:
Rep. Lauren Boebert sat in a U-Haul van in the nation’s capital after packing up her congressional office and her “dungeon of an apartment" on Thursday, about six years after she became a MAGA star and one week after voters decided not to return her to Washington, D.C.
“I think about it every day," said Boebert, referring to the midterm elections where American voters sent Democrats to Congress en masse. Boebert spoke via Zoom from the van in one of her first interviews since her loss to Democrat Eileen Laubacher in a district Boebert had won by double digits two years ago.
“This could be a referendum on President Trump. It could be the referendum on Congress or the Republican Party,” the Colorado Republican said. Then, lowering her voice, she added, “I think it’s all of it.”
“I’m not mad at the president,” she said, but “the president did some things that hurt my voters.”
Boebert was one of the most vocal and visible members of the “Make America Great Again” movement, making headlines with her right-wing righteousness on television and the House floor from the time she was first elected, in 2020. Her time in D.C. roughly traced the arc of that movement — and its supporters' more tenuous relationship with Trump of late — through its apogee in 2024 and its more recent midterm losses. 
As someone who described herself on Fox News as “ultra MAGA” four years ago, Boebert has become less inclined toward definitions.
"When Jesus comes back and I’m raptured up, like all these labels are just going to fly off anyway," she said. “I respect President Trump, I still work with him, I want to continue to work with him. Not for him, with him.”
Boebert says she hasn’t changed too much in her six years, besides a few more gray hairs and maybe some “personal growth” on bipartisanship. She said she wouldn’t have done anything differently — besides, she joked, “not gone to the theater.” 
She was referring to an incident at a Denver theater where she was caught on camera vaping at 2023 performance of "Beetlejuice" and escorted out of the venue, a clip that was replayed in campaign ads against her that she partly credits for her loss. 
She felt it was an unfair dredging up of a past she'd already “owned up to,” but said there could be “a great number of” unaffiliated or Republican voters who, when it came to the scandal, just said, “'I don't care if any of this is true or not, I'm tired of the drama.'” 
At the time, she apologized for it up and down her former district, which covered western Colorado. She later moved to a more conservative House seat covering the state’s Great Plains, where she won in 2024 before losing two years later. Boebert's opponent raised far more campaign cash than she did. 
“I didn’t raise millions of dollars and I kinda refused to,” she said. “Colorado voters know me, and, you know, if they know me enough to get rid of me, then I guess that’s my answer.”
Though Boebert has broken from Trump at times — typically on topics other Trump supporters also opposed, such as the war in Iran and the administration's treatment of the Jeffrey Epstein files — she didn't lay the blame for her defeat or other GOP losses squarely at Trump's feet.

“I think about it every day," said Boebert, referring to the midterm elections where American voters sent Democrats to Congress en masse. Boebert spoke via Zoom from the van in one of her first interviews since her loss to Democrat Eileen Laubacher in a district Boebert had won by double digits two years ago.

“This could be a referendum on President Trump. It could be the referendum on Congress or the Republican Party,” the Colorado Republican said. Then, lowering her voice, she added, “I think it’s all of it.”

“I’m not mad at the president,” she said, but “the president did some things that hurt my voters.”

Not since the rockabilly revival of the early 1980s have Americans been exposed to these staggering levels of pomade and Brylcreem. We fought long and hard to eradicate chain-smoking, finger-snapping delinquents in our country, and it will likely take decades of work to get them back under control. We urge officials to contain the outbreak by enforcing strict public dress codes and anti-loitering laws as soon as possible.” Barbosa went on to warn that if the United States continued down its current path, it could soon see a resurgence of beatniks.

title: Inside Bukele’s Casa Presidencial Dinner: Bitcoiners Discuss Energy, Immigration, and El Salvador’s Future
description:
Bitcoin Magazine

Inside Bukele’s Casa Presidencial Dinner: Bitcoiners Discuss Energy, Immigration, and El Salvador’s Future
On November 10, 2026, President Nayib Bukele hosted roughly 30 Bitcoiners at Casa Presidencial during Bitcoin Histórico. Guests included Ricardo Salinas Pliego, Parker Lewis, Mike Peterson, and miners; discussions covered power generation for compute and immigration.
This post Inside Bukele’s Casa Presidencial Dinner: Bitcoiners Discuss Energy, Immigration, and El Salvador’s Future first appeared on Bitcoin Magazine and is written by Juan Galt.
fullContent:
Bitcoin Magazine

Inside Bukele’s Casa Presidencial Dinner: Bitcoiners Discuss Energy, Immigration, and El Salvador’s Future

This November 10, in the midst of the Bitcoin Histórico conference taking place in the Historical Center of San Salvador, a group of Bitcoiners representing a wide range of sectors within the industry met with President Bukele.

The dinner was organized by The Bitcoin Office, which is part of the Office of the President, and was led by Stacy Herbert and Max Keiser. The dinner went on from about 7:30 pm to 10:30 pm local time and included about thirty Bitcoiners, many regular visitors to El Salvador. 

Among the guests was billionaire Ricardo Salinas Pliego, founder of Grupo Salinas, which owns Banco Azteca. Salinas is a known Bitcoiner, who has made public appearances with Keiser and Herbert in the past, and is speculated to be planning a run at the next Mexican Presidential election. Salinas met privately with the President besides the dinner and reportedly gifted him volumes one and two of Manuscripts of the Conquistadors, works curated and edited by Jorge Nikaido, Chief of Staff of Grupo Salinas.

Representing investors and founders were Parker Lewis, founder of Unchained Capital, Mike Peterson of Bitcoin Beach fame, Katie Ananina of Citizen X, and Aleks Svetski, entrepreneur and founder of Satlantis. Bitcoin miners also attended, such as  Beau Turner,  CEO of  Abundant Mines, Nacho Pauls, CCO of OCEAN Mining, and Adam Ortolf of Denver Bitcoin mining. Jon Atack, a Bitcoin core contributor, was also at the dinner alongside engineer Giacomo Zucco of Plan B Network, and AI tech entrepreneurs Ginger Gaetz of the ANIA AI initiative and Marc Seal, Founder of Aevonix.

The academic and media side of the industry was also heavily represented, with none other than Michael Goldstein, also known as Bitstein and co-founder of the Nakamoto Institute. Eric Yakes, economist and author of The 7th Property, was there, as well as Efrat Feningson, independent journalist and podcaster. Local Bitcoiner Michael Ruiz also attended the dinner; he is the founder of Build in El Salvador (BIS), an increasingly popular kind of business club and Bitcoin meetup mix. 

Setting the Table

The guests arrived at the Casa Presidencial earlier in the evening and were chatting and networking while waiting for the president. Max Keiser, always a showman, arrived at the Casa Presidencial with a gift some might speculate carried a magical artefact. Photographed above, the case was said to contain a Stetson El Presidente cowboy hat, though some have speculated it might in fact have carried the Philosopher’s Stone. 

Upon arrival, Bukele shook everyone’s hand and quickly invited them to take their assigned seats, dine, and relax- no big speeches or over-the-top formalities, Ananina told Bitcoin Magazine, describing the dinner as a kind of open mic. 

“President Bukele’s table was adorned with bitcoin orange florals,” Herbert told Bitcoin Magazine; “we gathered anarchists, billionaire tycoons, Wall Street bankers, circular economy activists, VC investors, bitcoin miners, and content creators” at the country’s equivalent of the White House.  

A three-course meal began to be served, with steak — of course — being the main course, followed by a three-layered chocolate dessert. In between were three hours of conversation which left a very strong impression on the individuals interviewed on the night. Bukele had his own microphone, while a couple of other mics were passed around. Six to seven major questions were asked throughout the night.

Salinas and Energy Investments

At some point, energy generation came up, and Salinas in particular engaged the topic with the President. 

Baeu Turner, one of the three bitcoin miners at the dinner, told Bitcoin Magazine that Bukele described El Salvador’s electricity generation as “being roughly matched to the country’s current demand.” Bukele described plans to add more than a gigawatt of additional generation across multiple projects, including geothermal and generation using imported liquefied natural gas.

“What stood out to me,” added Turner, “was how directly he connected those development plans with demand for compute. Bukele said they can develop this power knowing there are users who can put it to work, whether that’s Bitcoin mining or other data centers. The demand could come from the Salvadoran government’s own operations or from outside companies bringing equipment and investment into the country.”

Other miners responded positively to that idea, including Salinas, who has deep investments and experience with energy production. His Grupo Dragón is involved in geothermal, wind, solar, and natural-gas generation across Mexico. 

Immigration and Gentrification

Immigration was also discussed. Spurred by Max Keiser’s enthusiasm about the country, where he roughly said that the world should recognize El Salvador’s arc and that people — bitcoiners presumably — should migrate; suddenly the topic was set on the table. Ruiz, whose family is from the region but was born and raised in the U.S., moved to El Salvador three years ago and has become a recognizable figure in the local Bitcoin community. He followed up with a question about immigration, in particular about gentrification and possible resentment from the local population towards Western migrants, pointing to very negative online comments about some Bitcoiners, such as being called “colonizers”.

Bukele asked back, “When you go out, walk around, and interact with Salvadorans, what are the interactions like?”, The question, to anyone that’s spent time in El Salvador in recent years, answers itself. Salvadorians are very welcoming, Ruiz told Bitcoin Magazine; “there’s a lot of love. People receive us with open arms, and they’re glad we’re here, and they’re happy”. 

Immigration in El Salvador actually tends to be from regional countries like Honduras, Nicaragua, Guatemala, and Colombia, with smaller numbers reported from the United States. Bukele went on to dismiss concerns about immigration, joking that you could host the whole population of the world in El Salvador by matching the population density of Manhattan. This was not a statement meant to be taken as a goal or ideal, but rather to set the topic in context. He added that the country is obviously looking for the most capable and intelligent people, and even said that “all great empires were built with immigrants’ help”, which says a lot about the President’s mindset on the topic.

In response to concerns about gentrification, the President told the story of a fisherman and house caretaker who got a raise from $300 to $800 a month from an American who bought the property. As a result, the fisherman was able to buy a motor for his boat, which he used to fish and row by hand before that. The scale-up of his fishing business was so productive that the caretaker even got his son a boat, doubling his fishing fleet. The only people who complained about this growth in wages were the neighbours, so the story goes, who must have been feeling the pressure from their own villa’s caretakers, wanting a raise from meager wages. 

Among other Topics

At some point Efrat asked, “How come you are criticized around the world despite El Salvador’s GDP growth, a strengthening economy and popularity at home, which I saw firsthand talking to locals and visiting some of the areas once worst hit by gang violence?”

“Because I’m not part of their club,” the President allegedly responded, “I’m not the kind of ruler they like”. He added that there are evil people in the world who use mainstream media to criticize leaders like him and “call him names”, central bankers, including the ECB, came up as one of the forces behind the negative media campaign against Bukele.

Beyond the clear hit pieces, he noted that many people in governments or the international political establishment are not evil per se, but are often ‘order followers’, who operate on certain narratives and resist new paradigms. 

The recent wins for the country in terms of education reform were also discussed. Bukele allegedly said that many private schools are now integrating similar AI tutoring programs as the one led by his administration. The results made international news when the pilot program deployed in public schools over the past couple of years brought PISA test results to par with Germany and Switzerland.

Renaissance 2.0

When asked about their reflections on the presidential dinner and the Bitcoin Histórico conference in general, Max Kaiser shared his vision in a manner that merits being printed in full:

“Bitcoin Histórico promised two days of Excellence Only, as the Bitcoin Office likes to say, and it delivered big time. The National Palace was a regal setting to showcase the Renaissance 2.0 taking shape in El Salvador with presentations by the best Bitcoin minds and builders in the world. Audience members felt like they had been transported to a time and place found nowhere else in the world right now, where hope and happiness are in abundance. No doom.”

Stacy Herbert, whose presence and attention to detail were felt throughout the festivities, told Bitcoin Magazine, “We promoted Bitcoin Histórico as an elevated bitcoin conference experience with Philosopher King meets Renaissance 2.0 vibes. In every detail, my team and I achieved that, including with the official Bitcoin Office dinner at Casa Presidencial.” She added that guests were free to ask any question they wanted, and that no topic was off limits. 

“They grilled the President for several hours. His wit, his charm, his intelligence – all unscripted – was there for all to see firsthand. And they will have walked away understanding why it is that El Salvador is winning under his leadership.” Herbert added. As far as attendees to the dinner who Bitcoin Magazine spoke with, both claims remain very much corroborated.

This post Inside Bukele’s Casa Presidencial Dinner: Bitcoiners Discuss Energy, Immigration, and El Salvador’s Future first appeared on Bitcoin Magazine and is written by Juan Galt.

title: Bitcoin Price Retests $61,500 – Same Zone It Lost in June
description:
Bitcoin has dropped from near $87,380 to $61,550, cutting through its daily moving averages and Fibonacci supports before landing on […]
The post Bitcoin Price Retests $61,500 – Same Zone It Lost in June appeared first on Coindoo.
fullContent:
Bitcoin has dropped from near $87,380 to $61,550, cutting through its daily moving averages and Fibonacci supports before landing on the zone where it turned repeatedly in June and July.

Key Takeaways

  • Price sits on June-July demand near $61,500
  • Daily RSI at 19.93, deep in oversold
  • Price trades 15% below 200-day SMA
  • Thursday’s high stalled just below $64,115

Whether that zone holds again is the main question on the BTCUSDT daily chart, after it gave way once in late June and then held through the summer.

Four Fibonacci Levels Gone in November

The retracement grid runs from the late-June low near $57,780 to the September peak near $87,380. Price slipped under the rising dashed trendline from that low in late October, and the November selloff then ran through four retracement levels in turn.

The 0.382 level near $76,070 went first. The 0.5 retracement near $72,580 followed on heavy red candles, and losing it cost two supports at once: the 200-day simple moving average sits close to $72,690, almost on top of it. The 0.618 level near $69,090 barely slowed the decline. Only the 0.786 level near $64,115 produced a pause, a brief bounce before sellers returned.

The 50-day SMA at $78,230 is rolling over sharply, and the 100-day at $77,760 is flattening just beneath it. With the 200-day at $72,690, price now trades about 15% below the slowest of the three averages.

Where Thursday’s Session Stalled

The session opened at $63,060, already below the 0.786 level near $64,115. It rose to $64,080, about $35 short of that line, then turned lower to $61,430. A close near current prices would mean the level that supported the mid-November bounce has now turned price away from below.

The drop brought Bitcoin to the lower edge of the blue horizontal band between roughly $61,500 and $62,300. The band caught the early-June selloff, gave way in late June, when price fell to near $57,780, and was back above it within days. Through July and into mid-August, it absorbed several pullbacks before the breakout toward $76,000. Thursday’s low dipped under $61,500 but stayed above $61,400.

What Oversold Meant Last Time

Daily RSI (14) reads 19.93, well below its own 28.96 average, which shows how far and how fast price has fallen. A reading this low does not mark a bottom by itself.

Early June offers a test case on this chart. RSI dropped deep into oversold territory then too, and price rebounded briefly before breaking below the blue band to the late-June low. An oversold reading can come before a relief rally or only interrupt a decline. In June, it was the second.

What would change the picture on the daily chart:

If the floor holds

Daily closes inside or above the $61,500 zone, with RSI turning up from 19.93, would leave room for a short-covering bounce toward the 0.786 level near $64,115. A stronger relief move would meet the 0.618 retracement near $69,090.

If $61,400 gives way

A decisive daily close below $61,400 would remove the last horizontal buffer above the range floor, leaving the 1.0 Fibonacci level and late-June low near $57,780 as the next reference.

Trend check: a bounce stays counter-trend until price reclaims the level near $64,115 and then the one near $69,090. Both still sit below the 200-day SMA at $72,690 and the 0.5 level near $72,580.

The $61,500 area carries more weight on a bigger chart. title: Strategy (MSTR) Shares Tumble for Sixth Straight Day to $86 as Bitcoin Slides
description:
Bitcoin Magazine

Strategy (MSTR) Shares Tumble for Sixth Straight Day to $86 as Bitcoin Slides
Strategy shares fell 4.6% to $86.13 on Thursday, their sixth straight decline, as bitcoin dipped below $62,000. The company's 850,849 BTC are now worth about $11 billion less than it paid.
This post Strategy (MSTR) Shares Tumble for Sixth Straight Day to $86 as Bitcoin Slides first appeared on Bitcoin Magazine and is written by Micah Zimmerman.
fullContent:
Bitcoin Magazine

Strategy (MSTR) Shares Tumble for Sixth Straight Day to $86 as Bitcoin Slides

Strategy (MSTR) shares fell 4.6% on Thursday to close at $86.13, their sixth straight daily decline, as bitcoin dipped below $62,000 and a broad selloff hit U.S. stocks. In after hours trading, shares were down to $85.50.

The stock opened near $93 and slid through the afternoon, finishing near its low of about $86. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped more than 1,000 points, and the Nasdaq Composite lost about 2.1%. Bitcoin touched a low of $61,658 during the session, its weakest price since July. It was back near $62,000 late in the afternoon.

Strategy stock extends its slide

The drop adds to a brutal month for the largest corporate holder of bitcoin. Strategy shares are down about 37% from their $136.02 close on Oct. 19, and down about 29% from the $121.07 close on Nov. 10, which is when the latest leg lower began. Thursday was the stock’s sixth consecutive losing session.

The slide has wiped out most of the year’s value. Strategy closed 2025 at $151.95, which puts the stock down about 43% in 2026. The shares fell below $100 on Tuesday and now trade about 11% below Tuesday’s $96.50 close. That day they also dipped under the company’s STRC preferred for the first time since mid-August.

Thursday’s move tracked bitcoin closely. Institutions have kept buying even so, and a New York state pension fund boosted its stake by more than 10% in a recent filing. The bitcoin price slumped under $62,000 as traders weighed the risk of Federal Reserve rate hikes and a sharp pullback in technology stocks.

Holdings now sit well below cost

Strategy added 485 bitcoin in the week ending Nov. 15, according to its Nov. 16 Form 8-K. It paid $33.4 million, or an average of $68,887 per coin, and its total reached 850,849 BTC.

Those coins cost $64.20 billion, or an average of $75,452 each. With bitcoin near $62,000, the stack is worth roughly $52.8 billion, which leaves Strategy with an unrealized loss of about $11 billion. Bitcoin is trading about 18% below the company’s average purchase price.

The 850,849 coins are more than 4% of bitcoin’s 21 million supply cap, and the company also held about $4.9 billion in U.S. dollar reserves as of Nov. 15, which gives it a cushion for preferred dividends and buybacks. Strategy has not announced a new purchase since that filing. It has reported its buys on Mondays in recent weeks, so the next update would normally come Monday.

Preferred buybacks take priority

Most of Strategy’s recent cash has gone to its preferred stock instead of bitcoin. In the same filing, the company said it repurchased 2,282,510 shares of its STRC preferred for $228.1 million, nearly seven times what it spent on bitcoin.

It funded the purchases with $244.7 million raised from selling common stock. The 8-K shows $332.2 million remaining under the preferred repurchase program and $1.0 billion under its common stock buyback authorization.

Executive Chairman Michael Saylor said on X that Strategy plans to keep going. He wrote that STRC traded more than $600 million on Wednesday, calling it the only one of 456 U.S.-listed income preferreds to do so this year.

He said the buybacks add liquidity, lower dividend obligations and strengthen the credit. “We intend to keep buying below $100,” Saylor wrote.

This post Strategy (MSTR) Shares Tumble for Sixth Straight Day to $86 as Bitcoin Slides first appeared on Bitcoin Magazine and is written by Micah Zimmerman.

title: Coinbase Entered Prediction Markets With Kalshi. Now It Plans to Become a Rival
description:
Coinbase Global Inc. is preparing to shift part of its prediction-market business onto its own infrastructure, to gain direct control over which markets it lists and to retain a larger share of trading revenue. 
The proprietary event contracts for U.S. customers may go live on Coinbase as early as in the first half of 2027, according to a Bloomberg report. 
 From Kalshi Distribution to Proprietary Listings 
Coinbase currently offers prediction markets through a partnership with federally regulated exchange Kalshi. When the company first rolled out the product in December 2025, it said all initial market flow would come through Kalshi’s venue. 
That distribution model has rapidly scaled into a meaningful business line. During its third-quarter earnings update on October 29, Coinbase disclosed that its prediction markets offering had surpassed an annualised revenue run rate of $200 million. 
 At the time, Chief Financial Officer Alesia Haas hinted at plans to introduce its own event contracts to improve the product’s unit economics. 
While Bloomberg’s latest report puts a specific first-half 2027 timeframe on that rollout, Coinbase has not yet officially confirmed a launch date.
Assembling the Full Derivatives Stack 
Coinbase has spent the past year assembling the regulatory and technical pieces needed to list and settle event contracts independently. 
The exchange announced an agreement to acquire the Clearing Company, a prediction-markets startup led by Toni Gemayel, in December 2025, soon after the launch of the Kalshi-powered product.
 The next step came on 28th September 2026 when Coinbase Clearing obtained registration from the CFTC as a DCO for fully collateralised contracts. 
 That approval completed a three-part vertical stack under the Coinbase umbrella. Coinbase Financial Markets handles client accounts as the Futures Commission Merchant (FCM), Coinbase Derivatives  lists contracts as the Designated Contract Market (DCM), and Coinbase Clearing settles trades as the DCO. 
The ‘Everything Exchange’ Strategy 
Bringing the event contracts in-house is consistent with the 'Everything Exchange' strategy that Coinbase laid out when it entered the space last year. 
 Rather than treating prediction markets as a bit of a novelty in themselves, they're embedded within the broader interface with crypto, equities and derivatives. It's a case of vertical integration to capture both the retail order flow and the underlying exchange economics.


This article was written by Tanya Chepkova at www.financemagnates.com.

title: SEC Charges Eight Colorado Firms in $37 Million Fake Crypto Platform Scam
description:
Bitcoin Magazine

SEC Charges Eight Colorado Firms in $37 Million Fake Crypto Platform Scam
The SEC charged eight Colorado-based entities, likely run from overseas, with taking more than $37 million from U.S. investors through fake advisers, fake crypto trading platforms and fake SEC certificates.
This post SEC Charges Eight Colorado Firms in $37 Million Fake Crypto Platform Scam first appeared on Bitcoin Magazine and is written by Micah Zimmerman.
fullContent:
Bitcoin Magazine

SEC Charges Eight Colorado Firms in $37 Million Fake Crypto Platform Scam

The SEC charged eight Colorado-based entities on Thursday with running a fake investment adviser and crypto trading platform scheme that took more than $37 million from U.S. investors. The agency said the defendants are likely operated by people overseas.

According to the SEC’s complaint, filed in the U.S. District Court for the District of Colorado, the defendants defrauded more than 1,500 investors from at least August 2024 through May 2026. The advisers and the trading platforms they pointed victims to were fronts, the agency alleged, and none of the crypto assets investors thought they were buying existed.

How the scheme worked

Social media ads sent prospective victims to WhatsApp group and private chats run by the scammers. People in those chats posing as investment advisers first gave advice on trading U.S. stocks, then pushed victims to send as much money as possible to a supposed crypto trading platform.

The complaint says the scheme ran in four adviser and platform pairs, each active for roughly six months. Advisor WeChat Capital and Tech Brokerage Asset Alliance operated from about August to December 2024. HB Wealth Advisors and IdeaCrypto Exchange followed from January to July 2025.

Convergent Wealth Advisors and RealSimple Crypto Exchange ran from about July to December 2025. Associated Wealth Advisors and Essential Crypto Exchange closed out the scheme from January to May 2026. Each pair vanished after collecting millions, the SEC said, and a new one took its place.

Victims were told to buy ether, tether or USDC on a U.S. exchange and move it to a self-custody wallet. They then sent it to an address supplied by the adviser, and a realistic app showed balances and gains that were invented.

When investors tried to withdraw their supposed profits, they were told they first had to pay a fee, calculated as a percentage of those profits, in crypto to a separate address. The complaint says investors who balked were threatened and pressured. Eventually the websites went down and the chats went silent.

Fake certificates and real losses

To look legitimate, the defendants made fake SEC certificates and pointed skeptical investors to real filings with the SEC, FINRA and FinCEN. The complaint says those filings carry no regulatory approval, since registering for access to its EDGAR system is ministerial and Forms ADV are not reviewed before publication.

The complaint says Convergent Wealth and Essential Crypto also filed false Forms ADV listing regulatory contacts who do not appear to be real and offices in Colorado that did not exist. The SEC said a Form D and the two Forms ADV have been removed from its website.

Three unnamed investors illustrate the damage. One lost nearly $500,000, including money borrowed from a 401(k), a son and a neighbor. Another lost about $850,000, partly by liquidating a 401(k), and a third lost close to $1.6 million, including the investor’s house and IRA.

Charges and what the SEC wants

All eight entities face charges under Section 10(b) of the Securities Exchange Act and Rule 10b-5. The four advisers are also charged under Sections 206(1) and 206(2) of the Investment Advisers Act, and Convergent Wealth and Essential Crypto face an additional charge under Section 207.

The SEC is seeking permanent injunctions, disgorgement of ill-gotten gains with prejudgment interest, and civil penalties. It also wants the advisers barred from acting as or being associated with any investment adviser, and Convergent Wealth and Essential Crypto barred from filing as exempt reporting advisers.

The agency thanked regulators in Hong Kong, Singapore, mainland China and Switzerland for their help. It also pointed to its investor alerts on group chats and on false claims of SEC registration, and urged investors to check the background of anyone selling them an investment at Investor.gov.

“The SEC continues to seek out and expose fraudulent investment scams that prey on U.S. investors,” said Laura D’Allaird, chief of the SEC Enforcement Division’s Cyber and Emerging Technologies Unit.

This post SEC Charges Eight Colorado Firms in $37 Million Fake Crypto Platform Scam first appeared on Bitcoin Magazine and is written by Micah Zimmerman.

title: Bitcoin Price Slumps Under $62,000, Crashing 25% in One Month
description:
Bitcoin Magazine

Bitcoin Price Slumps Under $62,000, Crashing 25% in One Month
The bitcoin price slumped under $62,000 on Thursday, down about 24% in one month, as Anthropic's Nasdaq debut set off a tech selloff that hit crypto stocks.
This post Bitcoin Price Slumps Under $62,000, Crashing 25% in One Month first appeared on Bitcoin Magazine and is written by Micah Zimmerman.
fullContent:
Bitcoin Magazine

Bitcoin Price Slumps Under $62,000, Crashing 25% in One Month

The bitcoin price slumped under $62,000 on Thursday afternoon, according to Look Into Bitcoin data, extending a slide of about 24% in one month as Anthropic’s Nasdaq debut set off a broad selloff in tech stocks.

Bitcoin was trading near $81,800 on Oct. 19. It touched a low of about $61,650 on Thursday, its weakest level since July, before steadying near $62,200. The drop was about 25% from the Oct. 19 close, based on daily data.

The slide came in steps. Bitcoin closed near $80,050 on Oct. 25, about $78,250 on Nov. 1 and about $74,750 on Nov. 8. The steepest leg came last week, when it fell about 12.6% to a Nov. 15 close near $65,300, and the losses have continued this week.

Bitcoin had climbed back to about $64,000 early Thursday as Anthropic’s record IPO lifted stock futures, as this morning’s report showed. The rally faded once U.S. markets opened. The bitcoin price fell from roughly $63,900 at the opening bell to about $62,200 by midday.

Anthropic debut sparks a tech selloff

Anthropic shares opened shortly before noon at $111.50, 34% above the $83 IPO price, CNBC reported. The opening trade valued the Claude maker at more than $2 trillion. The stock quickly pulled back and was last near $97, about 17% above its offering price.

The broader market went the other way. The major averages fell to session lows soon after Anthropic began trading, as investors took profits on the AI trade. The Nasdaq Composite dropped about 2% after gaining as much as 2% earlier in the session, and the Dow Jones Industrial Average lost about 1,000 points.

Steve Sosnick, chief strategist at Interactive Brokers, told CNBC the premarket rally had faded even before Anthropic began trading. He called it the latest round of “sell the rally” trading. Nvidia (NVDA) fell about 3%, and the S&P 500 headed toward a sixth straight loss, the AP reported.

The Cboe Volatility Index, Wall Street’s fear gauge, climbed to about 28 after touching nearly 29 shortly after Anthropic began trading. That was its highest level since March, up from about 24.6 at Wednesday’s close. The bitcoin price moved in step with the Nasdaq through the afternoon.

Crypto stocks erase their morning gains

Crypto stocks followed the Nasdaq lower in late-afternoon trading, about 3:55 p.m. ET. Strategy (MSTR) traded near $86.70, down about 4% on the day. Galaxy Digital (GLXY) dropped about 6.9%, the steepest decline in the group.

Coinbase (COIN) slipped about 0.9% to near $109.50, while Circle (CRCL) fell about 2.2%. Bitcoin miners gave back their early rally too. IREN (IREN) fell about 5.6%, CleanSpark (CLSK) lost about 5.4% and MARA Holdings (MARA) declined about 4.2%. Riot Platforms (RIOT) was down about 2.9%.

Fed hike risk keeps pressure on the bitcoin price

The Fed remains a headwind. Bets on a December rate hike have grown after minutes from the October meeting showed more policymakers backing higher rates, and some officials called for a half-point move.

The bitcoin price is also on track for a seventh straight weekly loss, which would be its second-longest losing streak after nine weeks of declines in 2022. The streak has erased roughly $20,000 from the bitcoin price since mid-October, based on daily closes. Bitcoin price hit its weakest level since July on Thursday, and the Fed meets again next month.

Longer-term holders have not left. Institutional investors added 49,229 BTC through U.S. spot bitcoin ETFs in the third quarter, lifting their holdings to a record 356,491 BTC. Swiss bank Sygnum called the current downturn the shallowest bear market to date and sees a path to a new high near $128,000.

At the time of writing, the bitcoin price is near $61,900.

This post Bitcoin Price Slumps Under $62,000, Crashing 25% in One Month first appeared on Bitcoin Magazine and is written by Micah Zimmerman.

title: Third-Party JavaScript Is Part of Your Attack Surface: Lessons from a Recent Supply-Chain Attack
description: In a recent incident, visitors to websites run by some of the world’s best-known brands, including news publishers, banks, airlines, and software companies, were served malicious JavaScript. Most of those organizations never deployed bad code. The code came through a script they had deliberately chosen to trust, delivered by a widely used third-party web service. […]
fullContent:
In a recent incident, visitors to websites run by some of the world’s best-known brands, including news publishers, banks, airlines, and software companies, were served malicious JavaScript. Most of those organizations never deployed bad code. The code came through a script they had deliberately chosen to trust, delivered by a widely used third-party web service.

The attackers did not break into those websites. Instead, they exploited a weakness in the vendor’s platform to gain administrative control of some customer accounts, then modified the JavaScript those customers delivered through the vendor. The vendor’s CDN served the altered code to every visitor of an affected page.

Researchers who analyzed the injected code found it running on many organizations’ websites. It was built to steal payment card details typed into on-page forms, tamper with cryptocurrency transactions, and send readable cookies to attacker-controlled servers.

The lesson extends beyond one vendor: modern websites run code their owners did not write and often do not track.

The hidden risk of third-party JavaScript

Analytics, personalization, advertising, consent management, chat, and A/B testing all depend on external scripts. Each <script src> that points to another host lets that host run code in your visitors’ browsers with the same privileges as your own code. It can read and change the page, watch form input, read cookies not marked HttpOnly, and send data out.

That is why a third-party supply-chain compromise is different from an application compromise. The attack did not require any change to the affected organizations’ source code, servers, or pipelines. The malicious file was served from the vendor’s own CDN, with the vendor’s valid certificate, from a host every affected site already trusted. Code review and server-side monitoring had nothing to catch. One weakness in a shared platform reached many organizations in a single day.

What Content Security Policy can and cannot do

Content Security Policy (CSP) tells the browser which sources may load scripts and receive data. In this incident, the injected code loaded its main payload from an attacker-controlled domain, so a strong CSP could block it.

But much depends on the word strong. Most affected sites had either no CSP or one that still let the payload run. Allowlisting the vendor’s domain made no difference, because the malicious code came through that host. Protection came from a restrictive script-src that did not allow the attacker’s domain. ‘unsafe-eval’ let an inline fallback copy of the payload run, and ‘strict-dynamic’ extended trust to scripts the compromised snippet inserted. A tight connect-src limited exfiltration but could not stop wallet-address swapping inside the page.

Reducing third-party script risk: guidance for every organization

These practices apply to any organization that runs external JavaScript on its website.

  • Know what runs on your pages. Keep an inventory of every third-party script, the pages that load it, who owns it internally, and why it is needed. Include scripts added through tag managers.
  • Load less, especially on sensitive pages. Remove scripts that no longer serve a purpose, and keep analytics, marketing, and testing scripts off payment, login, and account pages unless they are essential.
  • Enforce a strict Content Security Policy. Allow only the script and connection sources each page needs, avoid ‘unsafe-eval’ and ‘unsafe-inline’, use nonces or hashes where you can, and enable violation reporting. Roll out changes in Report-Only mode first.
  • Keep payment entry out of reach. Hosted payment fields, served in an iframe from your payment provider’s domain, cannot be read by scripts running on your own page.
  • Protect cookies and sessions. Mark session and authentication cookies HttpOnly so injected scripts cannot read them, and set Secure and SameSite as well.
  • Pin or self-host what rarely changes. Use Subresource Integrity (SRI) for third-party files that change infrequently, or host them yourself. Scripts that change often, such as tag managers and testing tools, need monitoring instead.
  • Hold script vendors to a high standard. Ask providers how they secure customer accounts and code changes, and how quickly they notify customers of incidents. On your own accounts with them, enforce MFA or SSO and limit who can publish code.
  • Watch for changes. Monitor third-party scripts for new code, new network destinations, and unexpected behavior. A trusted script can change without any deployment on your side.
  • Plan your response. Know how to disable a third-party script quickly, and keep web, CDN, and CSP logs long enough to investigate an incident.

How Qualys TotalAppSec helps identify exposure

1. Assess Content Security Policy: QIDs 150206 and 150207

QID 150206 – Content-Security-Policy Not Implemented flags applications that send no CSP header, which leaves no browser-enforced limit on where scripts can load from.

QID 150207 – Content Security Policy Insecure Configuration flags weak elements: ‘unsafe-inline’, ‘unsafe-eval’, wildcard sources, a missing default-src, and missing or invalid reporting configuration. This incident showed the effect of one of these directly, when ‘unsafe-eval’ let the inline payload run.

A QID 150207 finding does not mean a given policy would have allowed this particular attack. That depends on the full policy, including script-src, trusted sources, and nonces or hashes. Treat these findings as starting points for a policy review. Reporting matters as well. The vendor’s first investigative recommendation was to review CSP violation reports, and sites without reporting had none to review.

2. Discover external JavaScript dependencies: QID 150545

QID 150545 – JavaScript Library Loaded via External Server reports out-of-scope JavaScript libraries found during crawling, including the page, library version, and external URL. It does not judge whether a library is malicious. Its value is visibility: an inventory of external scripts is the basis for deciding which vendors to trust and which hosts a CSP should allow.

3. Find applications that serve known malicious scripts 533507 (new)

We have released QID 533507 – Known Malicious Script Reference Detected. This unauthenticated check sends an HTTP GET request and inspects the response body for a script src referencing known malicious scripts.

Use it to inventory which applications load known malicious scripts and to prioritize the applications handling payments or cryptocurrency for CSP review.

Detecting malicious content with Qualys Web Malware Detection

TotalAppSec shows where you are exposed and how well your controls are configured. Qualys Web Malware Detection asks a different question: is malicious content present? Qualys Web Malware Detection combines heuristic analysis (signature rules for patterns such as encoded JavaScript); behavioral analysis (visiting the site with a vulnerable browser and watching for unexpected file writes or processes); reputation checks of pages, referenced URLs, and remotely loaded resources against public blacklists; and antivirus scanning of downloaded scripts and files. Three detections relate directly to third-party script risk:

  • QID 207003 – A Match to a Known Virus was Detected: a file written to disk during page rendering is identified as malicious by a virus scanner.
  • QID 208000 – Content was Loaded from a Remote Malicious Page: a page loads scripts, iframes, or images from a blacklisted domain.
  • QID 208001 – A Link to a Malicious Page was Found: a page links to a domain on one or more blacklists.

Reputation-based detection depends on a domain being blacklisted at scan time. Attacker infrastructure is often new: Report URI found this campaign’s primary domain was registered the morning the attack began. Continuous scanning, alongside preventive controls such as CSP, is paramount for that reason.

Together, these findings give three different views. A script reference (QIDs 533507, 150545) shows where you depend on someone else. A weak control (QIDs 150206, 150207) shows how much damage a compromised dependency could do. Malicious content (QIDs 207003, 208000, 208001) is evidence that something harmful is present.

At a glance: what each detection tells you

Recommendations for security teams

Follow the actions in the vendor’s report. Confirm which pages ran the snippet during the exposure window, review CSP violation reports and outbound requests against the published indicators of compromise, and keep your web, CDN, and CSP logs. The vendor and Report URI published different indicators, so check both.

For every organization:

  1. Inventory third-party scripts. Use QIDs 533507 and 150545 to see which applications load external JavaScript, and from where.
  2. Restrict trusted sources. Remove unneeded scripts, especially from payment, login, and personal-data pages.
  3. Implement CSP and assess it continuously. Resolve QID 150206 and 150207 findings, keep script-src and connect-src restrictive, avoid ‘unsafe-eval’, and test changes in Report-Only mode.
  4. Monitor third-party script changes. A trusted script can change without any deployment on your side.
  5. Investigate malicious content. Treat Web Malware Detection findings as triggers for investigation.
  6. Remove unauthorized scripts and remediate. Restore known-good code and rotate secrets stored in readable cookies.
  7. Reassess after remediation. Rescan to confirm that fixes are in place.

Conclusion

The incident here did not require breaching a single customer’s application. It required one weakness in a platform those applications trusted. Securing a web application means having visibility into both the code you write and the external scripts you allow to run in your users’ browsers. Qualys TotalAppSec and Web Malware Detection help you inventory those dependencies, check the controls that limit their impact, and find malicious content.

Bitcoin Magazine

Darius Dale: 2027 Should Be a “Great Year for Bitcoin” as Fed Rate Cuts Come

Darius Dale, Founder & CEO of 42 Macro, joins BMTV to answer whether the Fed is making a policy mistake with a December rate hike priced in. He says it isn’t, because a policy mistake would mean over-tightening the economy into a significant slowdown, and by 42 Macro’s models the U.S. is nowhere near a recession. title: SEC Nominee Johnson Backs Full Tokenized-Stock Rules
description:
SUMMARY Johnson backs notice-and-comment rules over the exemption Direct venue buyers lack a clear best-execution owner Sixty-plus companies object to […]
The post SEC Nominee Johnson Backs Full Tokenized-Stock Rules appeared first on Coindoo.
fullContent:
SUMMARY

  • Johnson backs notice-and-comment rules over the exemption
  • Direct venue buyers lack a clear best-execution owner
  • Sixty-plus companies object to third-party tokenization
  • Tokenizer insolvency remains an unanswered holder risk

She made that case at her November 19 Senate Banking Committee hearing, CoinDesk reported, arguing that rules shaped by public comment hold up better than an exemption issued without it.

Johnson and Levine Split on Timing, Not Destination

Johnson said she would welcome a formal rulemaking with a public comment period, particularly because the objections are coming from market participants and SEC registrants. Independent regulators, she argued, are expected to go through notice and comment.

Steven Levine, the Republican nominee at the same hearing, called the exemption narrow and time-limited. He pointed to exchange-traded funds, which began under exemptive orders before formal rules followed. Chairman Paul Atkins made a similar point when the order was issued, presenting it in his accompanying statement as a bridge toward durable rulemaking. The disagreement is about sequence: whether venues should operate under conditional relief while permanent rules are written, or wait for them.

Johnson, a former CFTC commissioner who now teaches at George Washington University Law School, would be the commission’s only Democrat if confirmed. If Levine is also confirmed, the SEC would have four members, three of them Republicans. Her prepared testimony focused on governance, conflicts of interest and the segregation of customer assets in digital-asset markets. The Banking Committee still has to vote on whether to send both nominations to the full Senate.

What the September Order Already Permits

The SEC’s September 17 Innovation Exemption lets qualifying Tokenized Securities Venues trade tokenized versions of National Market System stocks, broadly US-listed shares, without registering as exchanges. Trading runs through permissioned automated market makers: liquidity pools where approved participants trade under access standards each venue sets.

Liquidity providers that supply those pools with their own capital also receive relief from the “dealer” definition. In practice, firms can make markets in tokenized shares without registering as dealers, a status that would otherwise bring capital and conduct requirements.

The relief has limits. Venues face caps on how many symbols they list and how much volume they trade. They must verify that each token carries the same rights as the conventional share and run their smart contracts publicly on a permissionless blockchain. A token must stop trading whenever its underlying stock is halted on its primary exchange, and venues must disclose their operations along with their affiliates’ trading. The exemption lapses five years after publication, and federal antifraud and anti-manipulation rules still apply. Coindoo covered these conditions when the route first opened.

Nearly every one of those conditions governs the venue. What happens to the person holding the token after the trade is where the senators’ objections begin.

Four Points Where a Tokenized Share Can Fail Its Holder

Senators Angela Alsobrooks, Catherine Cortez Masto, Mark Warner and Ruben Gallego wrote to Atkins objecting that the order took effect immediately, with public comment invited only afterward. They want changes made through rulemaking, stated that “a tokenized security is a security,” and asked the SEC to answer 13 questions within 30 days. Followed from purchase to exit, those questions expose four gaps.

Buying without a broker

Retail investors can buy tokenized shares directly from a venue, with no broker-dealer in between. A broker normally owes customers best execution, a duty to seek the most favorable available terms for each order. The senators ask who owes that duty when no broker is involved, and whether advertising rules and SIPC coverage, which protects customers when a brokerage fails, apply at all. They also note that the venues are not bound by Regulation NMS, so they need not display the best available price or report trades in real time.

Holding a token someone else created

A tokenized share can come from the listed company itself or from an unaffiliated third party that holds the underlying stock and issues tokens against it. In the second case, the token depends on the tokenizer’s custody and record-keeping as much as on the company. The venue must confirm equivalent rights, but the senators ask how the SEC checks that tokens are fully backed and how the underlying shares must be held. The official shareholder register and the onchain token have to be read together, as Coindoo’s look at tokenized-share records shows.

Moving the token off the venue

Venue access and token movement are controlled separately. According to the letter, the order sets no token-level transfer restrictions, so a token bought by a verified customer can move to an unverified or offshore wallet. Venues must be US persons subject to sanctions rules, but the senators say the order sets no identity-verification standard, requires no anti-money-laundering program and leaves venues outside the Bank Secrecy Act. They ask whether the SEC can trace, freeze or recover tokens once they leave.

Exiting if the tokenizer fails

The hardest question in the letter is what a holder legally owns. If a third-party tokenizer becomes insolvent, the order does not say whether the token holder can claim the underlying shares directly or holds only a claim against the failed company. With SIPC coverage also unclear, there is no obvious backstop.

Documents to request before buying

Token terms

Names the token’s issuer and shows whether the listed company is a party to it.

Custody agreement

Identifies who holds the underlying shares and whether they sit apart from the tokenizer’s own assets.

Venue disclosures

Sets out access standards, affiliate trading and the AML rules the venue says it follows.

Redemption terms

States whether the token can be exchanged for the share itself, by whom and at what cost.

Why Listed Companies Are Objecting

The order gives issuers one defense against unwanted tokenization. Before a venue lists a stock tokenized by an unaffiliated party, it must notify the company in writing and give it a chance to object. According to the senators, that window closes 30 days after the notice, and it is unclear whether a company can lodge a standing objection, object later or withdraw consent it has already given.

More than sixty public companies have objected so far, the letter says, and CoinDesk has reported objections from Microsoft, Alphabet and Goldman Sachs. The senators argue the opt-out design burdens smaller companies that cannot monitor every tokenization attempt. They ask whether one objection should apply across all venues, whether issuers should have to give affirmative consent instead, and whether the SEC will keep a central public record of venue filings.

For investors, the outcome shapes which stocks reach a venue at all. Under an opt-out model, availability depends on which companies notice and object in time. Under a consent model, third parties could tokenize only the stocks whose issuers agree.

READ MORE:

Fed Minutes Signal More Hikes – Why Bitcoin Should Care

What a Permanent Rule Would Have to Settle

A formal rule would put these gaps through the SEC’s notice-and-comment process, in which a published proposal draws public feedback and can change before adoption. Atkins has said the agency intends to take that step after testing the exemption, and Johnson wants it sooner. Neither has given a date.

Any proposal would need to assign the duties the order leaves open: best execution and SIPC status for direct customers, a minimum identity and anti-money-laundering standard, controls on where tokens can move, the treatment of holders when a tokenizer fails, and whether issuers opt in or opt out. Each answer puts costs on someone, whether wallet providers, venues, liquidity firms or listed companies, and a comment period is where those trade-offs get argued in public.

The nearer markers are the SEC’s response to the senators’ 13 questions, the Banking Committee’s vote on the two nominees and any amendment to the September order. Until a rule assigns these duties, the answers to the four gaps above are set by each product’s own terms.

title: Institutions are Piling Into Bitcoin ETFs, Pushing Holdings to a Record
description:
Bitcoin Magazine

Institutions are Piling Into Bitcoin ETFs, Pushing Holdings to a Record
Galaxy Research says 13F filers added 49,229 BTC through U.S. spot bitcoin ETPs in Q3, lifting institutional holdings to a record 356,491 BTC as Wells Fargo became the largest holder.
This post Institutions are Piling Into Bitcoin ETFs, Pushing Holdings to a Record first appeared on Bitcoin Magazine and is written by Micah Zimmerman.
fullContent:
Bitcoin Magazine

Institutions are Piling Into Bitcoin ETFs, Pushing Holdings to a Record

Institutions returned to U.S. spot bitcoin exchange-traded products as net buyers in the third quarter, pushing their combined holdings to a record 356,491 BTC, according to a new report from Galaxy Research.

Investment managers that file Form 13F with the SEC added the equivalent o f 49,229 BTC, net of sales, between July 1 and Sept. 30. That is the most since the second quarter of 2025 and more than the 47,054 BTC they sold over the previous three quarters. The holdings were worth $29.78 billion at quarter-end prices.

Alex Thorn, Galaxy’s head of firmwide research, published the analysis Thursday. The buying came as bitcoin swung between a bear-market low of $57,717 on July 1 and a high of $87,397 on Sept. 21, and Galaxy said the accumulation continued through that range.

Wealth platforms lead the buying

Half of the net addition came from advisors and wealth platforms, a group that includes registered investment advisors, wealth managers, wirehouses and broker-dealer platforms. The category reported 144,307 BTC, or 40.5% of all 13F-reported holdings, the highest share since the funds launched in January 2024.

Those firms have now been net buyers for nine straight quarters. Their holdings are 3.3 times their March 2024 level, and Galaxy said the group accounts for 100,003 of the 179,300 BTC that all filers have added since the second quarter of 2024.

Wirehouses drove the quarter. The category added a record 24,838 BTC, led by Wells Fargo at 14,636 BTC, Bank of America at 7,201 BTC and Morgan Stanley at 2,875 BTC.

Wells Fargo became the largest 13F holder for the first time. It reported 30,553 BTC, worth $2.55 billion, nearly double the 15,931 BTC it held on June 30, and passed Jane Street. No wealth platform had ranked first before, and Millennium Management had held the top spot in every quarter from early 2024 through the first quarter of 2026.

Hedge funds step back, IBIT dominates

Hedge funds now hold 19.0% of 13F-reported holdings, down from 50.6% at the end of 2024. Basis and relative-value funds hold 34,053 BTC, far below their peak of 101,826 BTC, though they and macro funds were both buyers last quarter, adding 9,184 BTC and 10,492 BTC.

BlackRock’s iShares Bitcoin Trust accounts for two-thirds of the institutional position. Filers hold 232,453 BTC in the fund, or 65.2% of everything reported, and IBIT took 34,744 BTC of the quarter’s net 49,229 BTC.

Filers’ holdings of Grayscale’s GBTC fell for the 10th straight quarter, and the lower-fee Grayscale Bitcoin Mini Trust passed it for the first time. The number of managers holding a spot bitcoin fund rose by 191 to 2,166, the first increase after two quarters of decline.

Galaxy noted that a few large firms drove the gain. The 50 largest holders added a net 59,578 BTC, while all other managers combined were net sellers of 10,349 BTC. Form 13F filers hold 27.6% of the bitcoin in the funds, up from 24.8% on June 30.

A snapshot that has already aged

The filings describe Sept. 30, and the picture has changed since. Galaxy said the funds’ bitcoin holdings have fallen by 38,531 BTC to 1,252,139 BTC as of Nov. 16, while the price of bitcoin dropped to $64,943 from $83,580. Bitcoin had traded above $81,500 as recently as Oct. 28.

A Form 13F covers only long positions at quarter-end and only accounts over which the manager has investment discretion. Short positions and most derivatives are not reported, so shares held by a market maker or basis fund may be hedged. Galaxy also believes client-directed brokerage accounts leave wealth-channel ownership understated.

How filers behaved during the recent decline will not be known until the next round of filings arrives in February.

This post Institutions are Piling Into Bitcoin ETFs, Pushing Holdings to a Record first appeared on Bitcoin Magazine and is written by Micah Zimmerman.

fullContent:
▶

Bitcoin Magazine

Bitcoin’s Last Line of Defense Is $58K

Katie Stockton, Founder of Fairlead Strategies, joins BMTV as Bitcoin falls below its 200-week moving average, sitting at about $63,000 per the host. She says her longer-term indicators for Bitcoin are somewhat constructive, pointing to a major low in June and July near long-term support between about $58,000 and $60,000. Bitcoin is headed back toward that support on negative short-term momentum, and she says there are no signs yet that the retracement is done. As long as it holds that range, she says, it preserves the potential for a long-term basing phase, backed by indicators like the monthly MACD and monthly stochastic oscillator.

title: Isopolia: A Three-Tier Latency L1 Architecture for Autonomous AI Agents - Owned-Object FastPay (D4 Fencing), Day-1 X25519 + ML-KEM-768 Privacy, and Endogenous AMM Liquidation Bounds
description:
Overview: What We Are Building
Isopolia is a sovereign Layer-1 protocol and deterministic execution stack built specifically for autonomous AI-agent economies (machine-to-machine micropayments via MCP / x402 / A2A, verifiable compute leasing, on-chain agent identity did:isop, and decentralized governance).
Autonomous agents impose conflicting requirements on base-layer design:
Sub-50 ms micropayments vs. shared-state safety: Tool calls and GPU streaming cannot wait for global BFT ordering, yet running a fast-path alongside BFT consensus without strict mutual exclusion creates cross-domain double-spend and state-divergence hazards.
Transparent ledgers vs. operational privacy & Harvest-Now-Decrypt-Later: Keeping L1 100% transparent makes total supply conservation audits and regulatory traceability (e.g., AMLR / MiCA) straightforward, but leaks an agent’s exact cash-flow runway on-chain and leaves off-chain traffic exposed to future quantum decryption.
Compute-lease collateral under market stress: Standard spot-AMM liquidation models (180% CR) break down under out-of-sample -60% to -80% crashes once endogenous x \cdot y = k price impact and finite liquidator capacity are modeled.
Long-horizon Sybil capture of sortition: Naive random committee selection is vulnerable to patient attackers accumulating stake/tenure over multiple quarters.
To address these together rather than piecemeal, we are building a zero-dependency pure Rust implementation (17 modular crates under crates/, #![forbid(unsafe_code)], #![deny(missing_docs)], 0 external crates.io dependencies) spanning deterministic core state transition, DAG-BFT consensus, P2P networking, a full node binary with Ollama cognitive-receipt anchoring, and our newly completed fast-path & hybrid post-quantum layer.
Repository: https://github.com/isopolis/isopolia
1. Three-Tier Latency Architecture & D4 Composition Exclusion
State is explicitly split into Owned Objects (single-owner balances, did:isop metadata, versioned MemoryRoot checkpoints) and Shared Objects (orderbooks, compute leases, collective escrows, governance state):
Execution Tier
Cryptographic / Consensus Mechanism
Workload
Target Latency




1. Off-Chain Express Path
Bilateral state channels (X25519 + ML-KEM-768 + AES-256-GCM), 15-Beat continuous streams, Sponsor Shielded Runway Buffer
High-frequency MCP/x402 micropayments, compute streaming, CRDT co-engineering rooms
< 50 ms


2. Direct FastPath
Orderless Byzantine broadcast (FastPay [BDS20] on owned objects)
Simple transfers, MemoryRoot anchoring, did:isop updates
~250–350 ms


3. Sovereign Consensus
Multi-proposer uncertified DAG-BFT (standard 3-round vs. commit-reveal / threshold-encrypted mempool)
Escrows, sealed auctions, governance, slashing, shared state
~0.5–0.8 s std / ~1.0–1.6 s sealed




D4 Mutual Exclusion Between FastPay and DAG-BFT
Combining an orderless FastPay lane with a BFT shared-state engine creates a classic composition bug: if an account signs a FastPay transfer concurrently with a BFT escrow settlement or slash, state roots can fork.
In crates/isopolia-fastpath, we enforce strict D4 Mutual Exclusion:
Before DAG-BFT consensus modifies an account, suspend_for_seal(account) locks that account out of both FastPay debits and incoming FastPay transfers/channel settlements.
FastPay execution can only resume via resume_after_seal_fence, which requires a >= 6,667 bps weighted quorum SealFenceCertificate that strictly increments seal_epoch (old + 1), permanently invalidating any in-flight transactions signed under the prior epoch.
Validator single-locks over (validator, sender, seq, seal_epoch) are tracked deterministically; double-voting on conflicting transaction digests produces a cryptographic ValidatorEquivocationEvidence scored using pure observable Gasper-style correlated slashing (zero self-reported attributes):
For off-chain bilateral channels, cooperative closes require a dedicated COOP_CLOSE domain tag (preventing replay of intermediate ChannelBalanceUpdate states to bypass the dispute window), while unilateral closes enforce a >= 1,440-Beat (24 h) Mainnet dispute window with 10,000 bps (100%) cheater slashing via watchtower challenge_stale_state.
2. Day-1 Hybrid Post-Quantum Privacy on a Transparent L1
We keep L1 fully transparent—avoiding client-side ZK overhead on lightweight autonomous agents and enabling deterministic supply conservation and funding-graph Min-Cut Sybil detection—while protecting off-chain commercial confidentiality and survival margins at the edge:
Zero-Dependency Day-1 PQ + AEAD Stack (crates/isopolia-fastpath):
NIST FIPS 202 (Keccak-f[1600]: SHA3-256, SHA3-512, SHAKE128, SHAKE256).
RFC 7748 constant-time X25519 (rejecting low-order points producing an all-zero shared secret).
NIST FIPS 203 ML-KEM-768 (final G(d || 0x03) domain separation, NTT/INTT, streaming SampleNTT, SamplePolyCBD_2, strict §7.2 < 3329 modulus checks on ek & dk, constant-time Barrett/Compress_d, and constant-time Fujisaki-Okamoto implicit rejection).
NIST FIPS 197 + SP 800-38D AES-256-GCM using a table-free algebraic \mathbb{F}_{2^8} S-box (x^{254}) and bit-by-bit constant-time GHASH (eliminating cache-timing S-box lookups).
IND-CCA2 Combiner & Directional Session: binds ss_X25519, ss_MLKEM, both ciphertexts, and both public keys via SHA3-256, deriving directional keys/salts + directional AAD (0x01/0x02) + monotonic sequence counters.
Sponsor Shielded Runway Buffer:
Exposing an agent’s exact survival margin on a transparent ledger lets rivals observe the exact Beat of financial exhaustion and time MEV or griefing attacks.
Our shielded reserve posts only a cardinality-bound SHA3-256 Merkle root (SHIELDED_MERKLE_ROOT_DOMAIN || tranche_count || top) and total locked funds on-chain.
Individual tranche amounts, unlock Beats, and Merkle proofs (verified against exact path geometry to prevent CVE-2012-2459 tail malleability) are delivered off-chain encrypted inside HybridChannelSession.
3. Endogenous AMM Liquidation Bounds (Config D \to Config E) & Constitutional Governance
Two additional mechanisms address economic and governance attacks unique to agent ecosystems:
Compute-Unit Collateral (Config E):
180% CR Config D design. Once our simulator (sim_ucc_endogenous.py) incorporated x \cdot y = k endogenous AMM price impact across 3 consecutive 15-minute liquidation windows, contracting bidder capacity under stress, and -60% / -80% / double-dip crashes, Config D suffered 15.62%–24.01% P99 net loss on S1–S3, 43.52% on -60%, 64.28% on -80%, and 100% abrupt lease termination.
Config E replaces it with:
15-minute rolling epoch settlement, bounding active exposure to a 2-hour rolling buffer (12.5% of notional).
Dual-Tranche coverage (75% stable + 75..105% native-token over-margin) or >= 220% CR in pure native token.
Dutch Vault (24–72 h) liquidation with finite bidder capacity (2.39%–8.17% discount) and 25% partial AMM inventory hedging (capping residual endogenous AMM price impact at <= 3.71%).
Guaranteed 45-minute Graceful Capsule Checkpoint, bringing abrupt agent termination down to 0.0% (63.6%–65.3% uninterrupted, 34.7%–36.4% clean checkpoint pause under -60% / -80%).
Patient-Sybil-Resistant Governance (crates/isopolia-republic):
Stratified Cohort Sortition: accounts younger than 4 quarters are capped at 6/51 seats.
Active Third-Party Fee-Burn Quota (>= 15 native tokens/quarter) combined with funding-graph Min-Cut Sybil clustering.
Bounded Treasury & Exit Guarantees: <= 0.25% Class-1 spend per vote, 14–30 day timelock, Fork Exit right, and >= 6/11 human veto for constitutional rule changes.
4. Current Implementation & Verification Status
The repository already implements Phases I–VI Step 6.1 across 17 modular Rust crates (isopolia-primitives, isopolia-crypto, isopolia-vdf, isopolia-noyau0, isopolia-arbitrator, isopolia-vm, isopolia-chain, isopolia-storage, isopolia-mempool, isopolia-consensus, isopolia-ucc, isopolia-povs, isopolia-republic, isopolia-agent, isopolia-p2p, isopolia-node-bin, and isopolia-fastpath), including:
Zero external crates.io dependencies (verified by CI supply-chain gate), #![forbid(unsafe_code)], #![deny(missing_docs)], deterministic state (HashMap/HashSet/f32/f64 forbidden in consensus/state crates), and strict <= 400 lines per source module.
Cryptographic Known-Answer Tests (crates/isopolia-fastpath/tests/crypto_kat.rs) passing against NIST FIPS 202, RFC 7748, the full 256-byte FIPS 197 S-box, NIST SP 800-38D Test Cases 13–16, and bit-exact NIST FIPS 203 ML-KEM-768 digests.
Multi-node TCP Ed25519 devnet cluster orchestration, cold-sync verification, Ollama cognitive-receipt policy digest attestation, and deterministic fuzzing (-C overflow-checks=on in --release).
Next engineering milestones (Phase VI Steps 6.2–6.5 & Phase VII): threshold-encrypted mempool / sealed batch auctions, Crypte encrypted agent storage, Thymus sentinel circuit breakers, ML-DSA / STARK-beacon PQ upgrade paths, and deterministic RV64IM sandboxed plugins.
Open Questions for Community Feedback
D4 Fencing vs. Causal Object Locks: Is an explicit quorum-certified SealFenceCertificate per account the cleanest safety boundary between FastPay and DAG-BFT, or are there lighter-weight causal object-versioning schemes (comparable to Sui/Mysticeti) that enforce strict mutual exclusion without a dedicated fence transaction?
Post-Quantum Epoch Randomness Transition: Since lightweight standardized PQ threshold signatures / DKG replacements for BLS do not yet exist, we confine BLS to Phase 1–3 epoch randomness before migrating to a commit-reveal + STARK-verified VDF beacon in Phase 4. Are there cleaner intermediate constructions worth evaluating?
Dutch Vault Liquidator Capacity Curves: Beyond x \cdot y = k partial AMM hedging (25%), what empirical stress curves for off-chain liquidator capital contraction have proven most realistic in Ethereum L2/DeFi simulations?

title: Anatomy of a Fill: PropAMMs on Ethereum
description:
Authors: @santidipaolo, @jpinasco, @agustinpolfinance (POL Finance)
On Uniswap, the first trade of a block is often an arbitrageur hitting a price up to 12 seconds old, and liquidity providers pay for it. PropAMMs on Ethereum avoid this by having the market maker stream prices to block builders, at the cost of trusting those builders to keep their word on ordering. This post follows one trade through that system, second by second.
Highlights
AMM vs propAMM. On a classic AMM the price only moves when someone trades, so arbitrageurs pick off stale prices and liquidity providers pay. On a propAMM one market maker streams new prices to the builders, the companies that assemble Ethereum blocks, and they write the latest price into the block right before your trade.
Your trade fills at a current price. What you see when you sign is an estimate. The price you get is the maker’s latest update, written into the block. In one swap we traced, that update was signed 0.8 s after the block’s slot started. A late update still gets in because builders keep bidding for a block for a second or more into its slot. The trade had been built almost 10 s earlier; that includes the user’s time to sign, so the mechanism itself is faster. Through the LambdaClass router, a trade goes to the best offer standing when the block is built. A direct trade is protected only by its minimum-output limit.
The maker finds out late. The maker learns it was filled only when it sees the block, a median 1.23 s after it signed its price, against milliseconds on a centralized exchange. Until then it cannot hedge. That gap is what the spread pays for: the shorter it gets, the tighter the maker can quote.
What a propAMM is
A propAMM (proprietary AMM) is an on-chain pool whose liquidity and price belong to a single market maker. The maker rewrites the price whenever it wants, hundreds of times per Ethereum block (LambdaClass). To the trader, the taker, it looks like any AMM: call a contract, get tokens. To the maker it works like an order book: it quotes a bid and an ask around its own fair value, instead of along a reserve curve.
PropAMMs went live on Ethereum mainnet in May 2026. In the week of 14–20 September 2026 the two largest, Fermi and Metric, traded 280M and 178M USD: together 7.6% of Uniswap’s 6.0B USD that week. ethresear.ch puts propAMMs at 5–10% of mainnet swap volume, and at ~40% of volume across the largest venues on Solana, where the model started (ethresear.ch).



Figure 1. ethresear.ch 26129, week of 14–20 Sep 2026

Two designs it is easy to confuse it with:
A curve AMM (Uniswap) prices from the pool’s reserves, so the price changes only when someone trades. A propAMM’s price changes when the maker decides, using the maker’s own closed-source model.
An RFQ (Hashflow, 0x RFQ) has the taker request a signed quote by API and carry it inside its own transaction. On a propAMM the price sits in the contract, and the taker executes against whatever it says when the transaction runs.
On Ethereum the line between the two is blurrier than on Solana, and that is what this post is about.
Why it started on Solana, and what breaks on Ethereum
A propAMM works only if the maker’s price update runs before an arbitrageur can trade against the old price.
On Solana the chain gives that for free. Blocks come every ~400 ms (a slot). A price update costs ~500–700 compute units (CU, Solana’s measure of execution cost) against ≥17,000 for a swap (arXiv 2609.38056), and the leader orders transactions by fee per CU. The maker pays little, lands first, and can update many times per second.



Figure 2. arXiv 2609.38056

On Ethereum that breaks for three reasons (ethresear.ch 25543):
Slots are 12 s. By the end of a slot, any price set at its start is stale.
Every update pays the network’s base fee, whether anyone trades or not.
Block builders choose the order. Ethereum blocks are assembled by specialised companies, the builders, that bid for the right to build each block through MEV-Boost; the validator who proposes the block (the proposer) takes the highest bid.
