Layer 2s are a different case. Base produces 200 ms sub-blocks (Flashblocks) ordered by fee (Base docs), so the Solana approach roughly works there. This post is about Ethereum L1.
One trade, step by step
Five parties take part: the maker, the taker, an aggregator that finds the taker a price, the builder, and the proposer. The price the taker gets is the last update the maker sent the builder before the trade; what was on-chain when the taker signed plays no part.



Figure 3. One Ethereum slot · illustrative timing; rule from ethresear.ch 26129 and Titan docs


Before anyone trades. The maker reads exchange prices, runs its pricing model, signs a price update and streams it to Titan, Quasar, BuilderNet and Bombora, hundreds of times per block, one every few tens of milliseconds (PropAMM Factory). None of it touches the chain yet.
Quote. The taker’s wallet or aggregator asks for a price. The pool’s on-chain price is stale, so the aggregator simulates the trade against a preview the builder publishes: the pool as it would look with the latest update (LambdaClass).
Sign and send. The taker signs an ordinary transaction with a minimum output, minOut: if the trade would return less, it reverts. The transaction goes privately to the builders and skips the public mempool, where everyone could see it (Bombora docs).
Wait for a block. A new block comes every 12 s, so a trade that makes the next one waits up to 12 s, ~6 s on average. One that misses it waits for the following block. Meanwhile the maker keeps repricing, and the builder matches the trade only against an update at least 50 ms newer than the trade itself.
Block building. The builder writes the maker’s latest update immediately before the first trade against that pool; later trades in the same block use the same update. A trade sent through the LambdaClass PropAMM Router is requoted at this point against every propAMM, goes to the best offer, and falls back to Uniswap v3 if none beats minOut.
Inclusion. The block is proposed at the start of the next slot and reaches most of the network 1.5–2 s later. Titan built 44% of blocks in the period that A. Fuller’s memo covers, and carried 69% of propAMM trades (data memo).
Settlement. Tokens move inside the swap itself. The block becomes final two epochs later: 2 × 32 slots × 12 s, ~12.8 minutes.
Here is one real trade against El Zorro, the propAMM run by Zonda Markets.



Figure 4. Swap 0x395370f11681ae554d7308bd93be60ad8530a638727e617e75ac5b73fea04ed7 · El Zorro on-chain data

The fill is at a current price. The swap was built at 07:50:14 UTC; we read that from the transaction’s own deadline (method in the appendix). Its block’s slot started 9 s later, and the update it executed against was signed 0.8 s after that. The user signs after the transaction is built, and the chain does not record when, so part of those 9 s is the user reading the wallet pop-up and the mechanism itself took less than 9 s. What the user saw at signing was an estimate; the price came from an update signed at execution.
What stops the maker from showing one price and filling at a worse one depends on the route. Through the LambdaClass router, the trade goes to the best offer standing when the block is built. A direct trade to one propAMM is protected only by its minOut, which caps the loss at the trader’s slippage tolerance but does not guarantee the best price inside it.

Orders that settle through CoW wait for its batch auction, and take longer. Each line starts when the transaction was built, before the user signed, so it overstates how long the mechanism itself takes.

When the maker finds out, and why that sets the spread
The block is proposed at the start of the next slot, but nobody sees it at that moment. The proposer keeps collecting builder bids for up to ~1 s, sometimes longer, and the median node receives the block 1.5–2.1 s into the slot (ethPandaOps, 50,318 blocks). No builder sends the maker a fill notification, so the maker learns of its trade only when the block reaches its own node.



Figure 6. beaconcha.in (winning-bid categories, 950 ms timeout), ethPandaOps (50,318 blocks, 25 Apr–2 May 2026), Bombora docs; maker lane: El Zorro medians

El Zorro measured this over 24 hours of mainnet (14–15 October 2026, 404 WETH trades). Its quote was signed a median 0.76 s into the slot, and its node saw the block 1.23 s after the signature; for the slowest 10% of trades it took 2.18 s or more. For those ~1.2 s the maker holds a position it does not know about and cannot hedge it on an exchange. The taker is in the same spot on the other side: it cannot act on its new tokens until the block is visible.
That window is what the spread pays for. The maker quotes wide enough to cover how far the market can move before it hedges. Price moves grow roughly with the square root of elapsed time, so a shorter window lets the maker quote tighter for the same risk. In El Zorro’s data, Binance moved by more than its half-spread (0.90 bps; one basis point, bps, is 0.01%) during the window in 16% of trades; a 2 bps half-spread would have covered all but ~5%. Compare the same trade on Uniswap. The wallet simulates the swap against the pool’s current reserves, the user signs with a slippage limit, and the swap runs against whatever the pool holds when the block is built. If the output falls below the limit the swap reverts, and the user still pays gas.
The price at the top of each block is whatever the last trade left. When ETH moves on Binance, the pool stays at the old price until an arbitrageur trades it back, and that arbitrageur pays the builder to go first. The liquidity providers’ loss to these trades is called LVR, loss-versus-rebalancing (Milionis et al. 2022). Two more costs come with the design: a swap sent to the public mempool can be sandwiched, with a searcher buying just before and selling just after inside the user’s slippage limit, and the fee is fixed per pool tier (1, 5, 30 or 100 bps on v3) whoever is trading.



Figure 7. Illustrative path, no data; LVR as in Milionis et al. (2022)

On a propAMM the builder matches a trade only against an update at least 50 ms newer than the trade (ethresear.ch; Titan calls it freshness protection and lets the threshold be configured). The taker gets a price computed after it sent its transaction, and the maker is never stuck with the previous block’s price. The 12-second-old price that arbitrageurs pick off on Uniswap does not exist; what remains is the ~1 s window from the previous section. LambdaClass puts the consequence directly: “Because makers no longer carry the risk of stale prices, they can tighten spreads and improve their quotes” (LambdaClass).
A fresh price cuts both ways: if the market moves against the taker in the meantime, the taker gets the worse price, as with a market order on an exchange. It is still not a “last look”, where the maker sees an order and decides whether to fill it. The maker never sees the trade; the builder does the pairing.

On a centralized exchange (CEX) the trade is an internal event. The taker sends a market order; the exchange checks the balance it already holds in custody, matches the order against its book in microseconds to ~1 ms, and confirms in milliseconds. Settlement is a database entry; nothing moves on-chain until the user withdraws, hours or days later. The maker’s orders sit in the book at a known place in the queue, so the race is to get there first and cancel fast. The trade is final the moment the matching engine writes it, and the risk is the exchange itself.

On time to fill, an Ethereum propAMM is about four orders of magnitude (~10,000×) slower than a CEX (12 s against ~1 ms) and 30× slower than Solana. On the age of the price it executes against, the gap is much smaller: in El Zorro’s data the update was signed ~0.6 s before the builder sealed the block (median).

There are two clocks. The slot clock, 12 s, sets when the trade settles. The quote clock sets how old the price is: ~0.6 s when the block is sealed, ~1.2 s when the maker sees it. On Uniswap the two are the same clock, so a slow block means a stale price; a propAMM separates them, and that is what lets it work at Ethereum’s block time. The quote clock is also the one the spread pays for.

t = 0: getHeader. The proposer of slot N+1 asks the relays for the best header. The MEV-Boost default timeout is 950 ms, under a hard limit of ~1 s (beaconcha.in). Until the winning bid is committed, builders keep re-bidding, and Titan re-evaluates candidates on every quote update (Titan docs).
0 to 3.5 s: winning bid committed. beaconcha.in classifies the time from slot start to the committed winning bid as on-time (≤ 1,200 ms), timing games (1,201–2,600 ms) or aggressive (> 2,600 ms). Proposers who wait collect higher bids.
Sign, getPayload, broadcast. The proposer signs the blinded header, calls getPayload, and the relay publishes the block. No per-step latency is published. The relay knows which bid won at getPayload, before anyone else sees the block.
~1.5–2.1 s: the network sees the block. The median node sees it 104 ms (9 KB block) to 348 ms (238 KB) after first sighting, p99 427–1,248 ms; from slot start, the median is 1,505–2,122 ms (ethPandaOps).

a quote updater reads exchange feeds, runs a pricing model per pair, signs updates and streams them to builders, repricing “throughout the block”;
pricing models range from a fixed price to exchange prices with spreads that widen with volatility and inventory;
the propAMM contract reads the price from a Priority Update Registry and fills the trade;
operations: landing checks, circuit breakers, alerts, and a Postgres record of every published quote.

Wallets and aggregators set a swap’s deadline to the moment they build it plus a round time-to-live (TTL): 600, 1,200, 1,800 or 3,600 s. Taking the round value just above deadline − block time recovers the TTL, and deadline − TTL gives when the transaction was built. Bot flow drops out, because bots do not set the deadline that way. That leaves 39 WETH swaps: 24 direct and 15 CoW orders, whose time also includes CoW’s batch auction. The deadline is set before the wallet asks the user to sign, so any time measured from it includes the user’s signing time and is an upper bound on the mechanism’s own latency.

Compare the same trade on Uniswap. The wallet simulates the swap against the pool’s current reserves, the user signs with a slippage limit, and the swap runs against whatever the pool holds when the block is built. If the output falls below the limit the swap reverts, and the user still pays gas.

The price at the top of each block is whatever the last trade left. When ETH moves on Binance, the pool stays at the old price until an arbitrageur trades it back, and that arbitrageur pays the builder to go first. The liquidity providers’ loss to these trades is called LVR, loss-versus-rebalancing (Milionis et al. 2022). Two more costs come with the design: a swap sent to the public mempool can be sandwiched, with a searcher buying just before and selling just after inside the user’s slippage limit, and the fee is fixed per pool tier (1, 5, 30 or 100 bps on v3) whoever is trading.


Figure 7. Illustrative path, no data; LVR as in Milionis et al. (2022)

On a propAMM the builder matches a trade only against an update at least 50 ms newer than the trade (ethresear.ch; Titan calls it freshness protection and lets the threshold be configured). The taker gets a price computed after it sent its transaction, and the maker is never stuck with the previous block’s price. The 12-second-old price that arbitrageurs pick off on Uniswap does not exist; what remains is the ~1 s window from the previous section. LambdaClass puts the consequence directly: “Because makers no longer carry the risk of stale prices, they can tighten spreads and improve their quotes” (LambdaClass).

A fresh price cuts both ways: if the market moves against the taker in the meantime, the taker gets the worse price, as with a market order on an exchange. It is still not a “last look”, where the maker sees an order and decides whether to fill it. The maker never sees the trade; the builder does the pairing.

The same trade on a centralized exchange

On a centralized exchange (CEX) the trade is an internal event. The taker sends a market order; the exchange checks the balance it already holds in custody, matches the order against its book in microseconds to ~1 ms, and confirms in milliseconds. Settlement is a database entry; nothing moves on-chain until the user withdraws, hours or days later. The maker’s orders sit in the book at a known place in the queue, so the race is to get there first and cancel fast. The trade is final the moment the matching engine writes it, and the risk is the exchange itself.

The clock, side by side

On time to fill, an Ethereum propAMM is about four orders of magnitude (~10,000×) slower than a CEX (12 s against ~1 ms) and 30× slower than Solana. On the age of the price it executes against, the gap is much smaller: in El Zorro’s data the update was signed ~0.6 s before the builder sealed the block (median).


Figure 8. ethresear.ch 26129 (Solana, Ethereum slots), Base docs (Flashblocks), Ethereum finality = 2 epochs × 32 slots × 12 s; CEX range is a third-party estimate

There are two clocks. The slot clock, 12 s, sets when the trade settles. The quote clock sets how old the price is: ~0.6 s when the block is sealed, ~1.2 s when the maker sees it. On Uniswap the two are the same clock, so a slow block means a stale price; a propAMM separates them, and that is what lets it work at Ethereum’s block time. The quote clock is also the one the spread pays for.

CEX Uniswap propAMM (Ethereum)
Where the price lives The exchange’s order book Pool reserves (curve) Contract, rewritten by the maker
Who sets the order of trades Matching engine, price-time Builder, for its own profit Builder, update before trade
Age of the price at fill Microseconds Up to 12 s Signed after the trade arrives
Time to fill Microseconds to ms Next block (12 s) or later Next block (12 s) or later
Maker learns of the fill Milliseconds Not applicable (passive pool) ~1.2 s after its quote (median)
What you trust The exchange Nothing on ordering Builders to honour the rule

In numbers

Sources here are a single-author memo or interested parties.

Metric Value Source
ETH/USDC full spread (ask − bid) around the maker’s own mid, smallest size, single snapshot 1 Sep 2026 0.86 bps (Metric) to 4.20 bps (bopAMM); Fermi 2.34 bps A. Fuller memo
Capital turnover per day Fermi ~23× its 5.4M USD of liquidity; Uniswap v3 on the same pairs 0.6× its 319M USD. Memo’s own period: with the September volume above, Fermi’s would be ~7× A. Fuller memo
Gas, price update vs swap (measured on Base) ~27–33K vs 200–400K arXiv
LambdaClass Router flow ~13M USD across ~1,000 swaps per day (22 Sep 2026) LambdaClass

The turnover row is the business model: the maker does not park liquidity in the pool, it refills from its exchange inventory, so a few million dollars of capital carry volume of the same order as Uniswap’s pools on those pairs.

The trade-off

The underlying difference is who controls the order between the maker’s price and the trade: the matching engine on a CEX, nobody on Uniswap, the builder on an Ethereum propAMM. The propAMM gives the maker back its ability to react, and shrinks its exposure from a 12-second-old price to the ~1 second until it sees the block. The cost is an intermediary back in the ordering: four private builders that promise to write the update first, with nothing in the protocol enforcing it.

Appendix: for builders and market makers

A1. The slot boundary, step by step

  1. End of slot N: last updates and takes. Each maker update is valid for a single block, the next one (Bombora docs). A take is eligible only against a quote received more than the freshness buffer after it: taker_received_at + freshness_buffer < quote_received_at, using only the builder’s own receive timestamps.
  2. t = 0: getHeader. The proposer of slot N+1 asks the relays for the best header. The MEV-Boost default timeout is 950 ms, under a hard limit of ~1 s (beaconcha.in). Until the winning bid is committed, builders keep re-bidding, and Titan re-evaluates candidates on every quote update (Titan docs).
  3. 0 to 3.5 s: winning bid committed. beaconcha.in classifies the time from slot start to the committed winning bid as on-time (≤ 1,200 ms), timing games (1,201–2,600 ms) or aggressive (> 2,600 ms). Proposers who wait collect higher bids.
  4. Sign, getPayload, broadcast. The proposer signs the blinded header, calls getPayload, and the relay publishes the block. No per-step latency is published. The relay knows which bid won at getPayload, before anyone else sees the block.
  5. ~1.5–2.1 s: the network sees the block. The median node sees it 104 ms (9 KB block) to 348 ms (238 KB) after first sighting, p99 427–1,248 ms; from slot start, the median is 1,505–2,122 ms (ethPandaOps).
  6. t = 4 s: attestation deadline. Attesters vote with or without the block. Proposing at ~3–3.5 s already costs ~10% wrong-head votes (ethresear.ch 20272, Jul–Aug 2024).
  7. The maker learns of the fill. Neither Titan nor Bombora documents a fill notification; Bombora’s ACK only confirms the update was forwarded, and stale or reverting quotes are dropped silently. PropAMM Factory runs per-block landing checks (LambdaClass). In El Zorro’s 24 h sample its node saw the block a median 1.99 s into slot N+1 (p10 1.62 s, p90 3.41 s) and its pusher ~160 ms later. Blocks arrive in two regimes, around 1.7–1.8 s and 3.2–3.4 s; when the block is sealed late the builder takes a later signature, so the quote’s age stays the same.
  8. Rebalance. The maker hedges on a CEX in milliseconds or tops up on-chain inventory. No public source measures maker hedging latency. On Base, Tessera refills from opposite on-chain flow without hedging (arXiv).

A2. How fresh in practice

El Zorro, 24 h of mainnet, 14–15 Oct 2026, 404 WETH inclusions. The included quote was signed a median 0.76 s after the slot started. The builder sealed ~0.61 s after the signature (an upper bound, from Titan’s public stream). El Zorro’s node saw the block 1.23 s after the signature (p10 0.84 s, p90 2.18 s). Titan, BuilderNet and Quasar give the same distribution, and nothing is included younger than 0.5 s.

Over that window ETHUSDT on Binance moved a median 0.04 bps and 1.72 bps at p90, against a published half-spread of 0.90 bps (median). The move exceeded the half-spread in 16% of inclusions; a 2 bps half-spread would cut that to ~5%. Stablecoin pairs are a separate population: the quote is re-signed only when the price moves, so a median age of 6.9 s costs nothing.

A3. How a maker implements it: El Zorro

El Zorro runs on PropAMM Factory, LambdaClass’s open-source kit:

  • a quote updater reads exchange feeds, runs a pricing model per pair, signs updates and streams them to builders, repricing “throughout the block”;
  • pricing models range from a fixed price to exchange prices with spreads that widen with volatility and inventory;
  • the propAMM contract reads the price from a Priority Update Registry and fills the trade;
  • operations: landing checks, circuit breakers, alerts, and a Postgres record of every published quote.

A4. How we time a transaction

The chain does not record when a transaction was built or signed. Wallets and aggregators set a swap’s deadline to the moment they build it plus a round time-to-live (TTL): 600, 1,200, 1,800 or 3,600 s. Taking the round value just above deadline − block time recovers the TTL, and deadline − TTL gives when the transaction was built. Bot flow drops out, because bots do not set the deadline that way. That leaves 39 WETH swaps: 24 direct and 15 CoW orders, whose time also includes CoW’s batch auction. The deadline is set before the wallet asks the user to sign, so any time measured from it includes the user’s signing time and is an upper bound on the mechanism’s own latency.

A5. Full comparison

CEX AMM (Uniswap v3/v4) propAMM (Ethereum L1) RFQ (Hashflow, 0x RFQ)
Where the price lives Matching engine’s book Pool reserves (curve) Contract state, rewritten by the maker Off-chain signed quote
Who moves it Maker, at will Only trades Maker, streamed to the builder Maker, on request
Who orders Matching engine, price-time Builder, for its own profit Builder, update-before-take rule Taker carries the quote in its tx
Age of the price at fill µs Up to 12 s (last trade) ≥ 50 ms newer than the take Up to quote expiry
Time to fill ~1 ms Next slot (12 s) or later Next slot (12 s) or later Next slot (12 s) or later
Maker learns of the fill Milliseconds Not applicable (passive LP) ~1.2 s after its quote (median) When the block is visible
Maker’s adverse selection Cancel race LVR to the arbitrageur Window between update and take Quote validity window
Custody The exchange On-chain, taker On-chain, taker On-chain, taker
Settlement Internal ledger, immediate Atomic on-chain Atomic on-chain Atomic on-chain
Trust assumption Exchange solvency None on ordering Builder honours the rule None on ordering

fullContent:
What if Bitcoin’s next major rally isn’t just another cryptocurrency bull run, but the start of a fundamental shift in how the world’s largest economies view money? Perplexity AI predicts Bitcoin’s 2027 price target, offering an in-depth look at how it could reach such an insane level.

Sovereign adoption, rising institutional demand, monetary easing, and growing concerns over government debt could create the conditions for an extraordinary Bitcoin rally in 2027.

(SOURCE: Perplexity AI Predicts a Bullish BTC Price Target for 2027)

While a seven-figure price for Bitcoin may still seem outrageous, the key factors supporting such a valuation are becoming harder to ignore. With a fixed supply of 21 million coins, an expanding institutional infrastructure, and governments starting to consider Bitcoin as a strategic reserve asset, the long-term investment outlook is evolving.

However, reaching $1M would require an unprecedented influx of capital. Could 2027 be the year when Bitcoin takes a giant leap toward that milestone? A particularly bullish scenario might drive Bitcoin’s value much higher than many investors currently expect.

Could Governments Start Treating Bitcoin Like Digital Gold?

(SOURCE: CoinGecko)

One of the most significant potential catalysts is sovereign adoption. In March 2025, US President Donald Trump signed an executive order establishing a Strategic Bitcoin Reserve, creating an official framework for holding government-owned Bitcoin rather than automatically selling seized assets. However, the proposed reserve remains subject to administrative and legislative uncertainty.

The bigger development would be an announcement that the US intends to acquire additional Bitcoin through a government-backed purchasing program.

If other major economies followed suit, the resulting competition for a limited supply could fundamentally change BTC’s valuation.

Institutional demand is another important consideration. US spot Bitcoin ETFs added approximately 79,800 BTC during the third quarter of 2026, almost twice the amount newly mined during the same period. This demonstrates how quickly institutional investment vehicles can absorb available supply when demand returns.

Imagine that trend accelerating throughout 2027, with pension funds, sovereign wealth funds and major asset managers increasing their allocations. Bitcoin could experience a substantial supply-demand imbalance.

EXPLORE: 9+ Best High-Risk, High-Reward Crypto to Buy in 2026

Perplexity AI Predicts The Macroeconomic Perfect Storm Could Spark a Parabolic BTC Run

Bitcoin’s next major rally could also depend on developments outside the cryptocurrency industry. Government debt, persistent fiscal deficits, and concerns surrounding fiat currency purchasing power could strengthen the argument for scarce alternative assets.

A particularly bullish macroeconomic scenario would involve central banks cutting interest rates as inflation moderates, alongside renewed liquidity injections and an expanding global money supply.

Historically, Bitcoin has benefited from improving liquidity conditions, although its relationship with global money supply is not guaranteed to persist. Fidelity Digital Assets has highlighted how the relationship has become less reliable during recent market conditions.

If financial conditions become significantly more accommodative in 2027, risk appetite could return to cryptocurrency markets. Another potential catalyst is the next Bitcoin halving, expected in 2028. Although it falls outside the 2027 forecast, markets could begin pricing in its impact beforehand, particularly as investors anticipate another reduction in newly issued BTC.

Combined, these developments could create a powerful narrative around Bitcoin’s increasingly scarce supply and growing monetary significance.

What Does the Long-Term Technical Picture Suggest?

Market Cap

From a higher-timeframe perspective, Bitcoin’s ability to establish a sustained bullish structure will be essential.

Rather than focusing on daily fluctuations, investors should watch the monthly chart for higher highs and higher lows, along with improving momentum indicators and sustained trading volume.

A decisive move above previous cycle resistance zones, followed by successful retests, could signal the beginning of another major expansion phase.

The $200,000–$300,000 region would represent an important psychological milestone in a bullish scenario, while sustained institutional accumulation could potentially support a move beyond those levels. However, a seven-figure valuation would require much more than a conventional bull market.

Could Bitcoin Reach $500,000 in 2027?

For Bitcoin to reach $1M, its market capitalization would approach $20 trillion, based on a circulating supply of roughly 20 million coins. That would put it in direct competition with gold as a global store of value.

While not impossible over a longer timeframe, achieving that valuation in 2027 would require an extraordinary convergence of events.

My bullish Bitcoin prediction for 2027 is $500,000, with a potential trading range of $350,000–$500,000 under an exceptionally favorable combination of institutional adoption, sovereign accumulation, and improving global liquidity.

I believe $1M remains a longer-term possibility, but $500,000 is an ambitious yet more defensible target for the next major market expansion.

If governments begin competing for Bitcoin, institutional demand accelerates, and central banks turn towards easier monetary policy, the road to seven figures could become considerably shorter than many expect.

XRP Has an Institutional Edge, But Garlinghouse Believes Wall Street Is Pulling Liquidity Away
description:
Garlinghouse links XRP price weakness to liquidity flowing into the Anthropic IPO as XRPL secures a major institutional milestone.
The post XRP Has an Institutional Edge, But Garlinghouse Believes Wall Street Is Pulling Liquidity Away appeared first on Cryptonews.
fullContent:
The XRP price is struggling to take advantage of institutional credibility for the ledger. Ripple CEO Brad Garlinghouse has another explanation: Wall Street is pulling liquidity toward blockbuster IPOs.

The XRP Ledger Foundation assessed the network against all ten principles in the Global Layer One (GL1) Market Infrastructure Toolkit. CertiK independently verified the network’s evidence under the Architecture and Resiliency principles.

Garlinghouse said investors have been moving money out of crypto, including XRP, to fund major listings. He expects the market to recover after Anthropic’s debut, just as it did following SpaceX’s IPO.

XRPL Adds an Institutional Credential

The GL1 toolkit gives financial institutions a common framework for assessing digital infrastructure. It has ten principles that cover governance, legal foundations, settlement finality, architecture, economic models, resilience, access, interoperability, privacy, and operations.

This makes the assessment relevant to banks exploring tokenized markets. Institutions need to understand how networks handle operational risk, governance, and settlement before building financial products on them.

XRPL’s case is notable because it is public and permissionless. Traditional financial networks often operate behind controlled access. Public blockchains must show how risks are handled across distributed governance, protocol upgrades, and open participation.

The Foundation assessed XRPL against all ten principles. It also supplied supporting evidence for each control. CertiK then examined the Architecture and Resiliency sections, using code, configurations, logs, and test results.

CertiK said it reviewed all 112 controls in the toolkit. Its technical verification focused on those suitable for independent assessment. The firm also verified Partior’s self-attestation under the same two principles.

The XRPL Foundation called it the first such verification for a public, permissionless Layer 1. The milestone gives institutions a structured reference when evaluating networks for tokenized deposits, stablecoins, funds, and other assets.

That is useful progress for XRPL’s institutional pitch. Risk and compliance teams can now examine evidence against familiar market-infrastructure standards. They have more than a blockchain’s own description of its capabilities.

Discover: The Best Token Presales

Garlinghouse Looks to Anthropic IPO for XRP Price Relief

Xrp (XRP)
24h7d30d1yAll time

In the interview, Garlinghouse addressed the gap between Ripple’s expansion and XRP price performance. He said the SpaceX IPO triggered a similar pullback as investors shifted liquidity out of crypto. He specifically named Bitcoin and XRP among the assets affected.

Investors moved capital from liquid crypto markets into the highly anticipated SpaceX listing, he said. Garlinghouse sees the same pattern ahead of Anthropic’s debut.

Anthropic priced its shares at $83 and began trading on Nasdaq under the ticker ANT on Thursday. The offering covers 980 million shares, and the deal is expected to close Friday, November 20.

“What we saw after the SpaceX IPO was a rally in the crypto markets,” Garlinghouse said. “I think you’ll see that happen here as well.”

He also expects digital assets to stop moving in lockstep. In his view, real utility and demand will increasingly separate stronger projects from speculative tokens. That puts the XRP price debate back on XRPL’s ability to attract activity.

Discover: The Crypto Presales This Q4 2026

Bitcoin Hyper Races Toward Presale Deadline With $33M Raised

Bitcoin Hyper is chasing a similar infrastructure opportunity as XRPL, this time around Bitcoin. Its Layer 2 combines Solana Virtual Machine (SVM) technology with Bitcoin settlement, aiming to bring faster transactions, DeFi applications, and staking to the Bitcoin ecosystem.

The project has already rolled out its public testnet, explorer, wallet, faucet, bridge, and staking portal. These releases give developers and early users a working environment to explore before the planned mainnet rollout.

The presale has raised more than $33.2 million, with HYPER priced at just $0.0136. The November 26 deadline is now approaching, leaving less than a week before the scheduled presale close.

XRPL’s latest institutional milestone shows how infrastructure improvements can strengthen a blockchain’s appeal to financial players. Bitcoin Hyper is pursuing a different route, building an execution layer that could make Bitcoin more useful across payments and decentralized finance.

If Bitcoin Layer 2 adoption gains traction, projects delivering faster execution and financial applications could attract growing institutional attention. Bitcoin Hyper is positioning itself ahead of that opportunity, with its presale entering its final stretch.

fullContent:
LEWISTON, ME—Admitting that the wet sounds of it crawling around at night were far preferable to the racket of squeaking and scratching in the walls, local man Scott Burgess told reporters Thursday the creature in his basement was really helping with the rat problem. “When I saw that thing’s tail whip around a dark corner of the cellar, I thought it might be a problem, but it seems to have scared off a lot of the rats,” said Burgess, who added that people often only think about the evil aspects of basement creatures and fail to consider the role they play in keeping pest populations in check. “Our house is more peaceful now that it’s lurking down there. There are drawbacks, of course—my wife went down to do laundry the other day and hasn’t been the same since—but at least I don’t have to drop $500 on an exterminator. Sometimes you’ll step in a pool of bile and have to kick your shoes off before it burns through the soles, but that’s a small price to pay to not have rat droppings everywhere. And while it’s a little gross throwing out the larger and larger exoskeletons it keeps shedding, it’s still better than cleaning out a glue trap.” At press time, Burgess was hoping the rat problem would be solved for good now that he found two sets of smaller claw prints trailing the larger one.

title: Tether Pushes Back Against S&P as USDT Reserve Maintains Lowest Stability Assessment
description: Tether pushes back against S&P Global Ratings after the agency maintained its lowest stability assessment for USDT, pointing to a growing share of higher-risk assets in the stablecoin’s reserves and continuing concerns about transparency. In its latest assessment, published November 18, S&P kept USDT’s ability to maintain its dollar peg at 5 (weak), the lowest […]
fullContent:
Tether pushes back against S&P Global Ratings after the agency maintained its lowest stability assessment for USDT, pointing to a growing share of higher-risk assets in the stablecoin’s reserves and continuing concerns about transparency.

In its latest assessment, published November 18, S&P kept USDT’s ability to maintain its dollar peg at 5 (weak), the lowest score on its five-point scale. The rating remains unchanged from November 2025, when the agency first downgraded the stablecoin. Tether rejected the assessment, arguing that the problem lies with S&P’s evaluation framework rather than the composition of its reserves. The company also referenced The Big Short, the film about the 2008 financial crisis, in its response to the agency’s findings.

Higher-Risk Assets Account for 28% of USDT in Circulation

S&P’s latest concerns center on the changing composition of Tether’s reserves. According to the report, higher-risk holdings, including Bitcoin, gold, public equities, secured loans and corporate bonds, represented approximately 28% of USDT in circulation as of September 30.

That figure increased from 24% a year earlier, indicating a growing exposure to assets whose values can fluctuate with market conditions. S&P warned that a significant decline in the value of these holdings could leave USDT undercollateralized, particularly if several reserve assets experienced losses at the same time.

The company also argued that the agency’s own history demonstrated weaknesses in traditional financial risk assessments. Tether’s September 30 reserve report, attested by BDO, showed approximately $191.5 billion in assets against $183.5 billion in liabilities. This left the company with roughly $7.95 billion in excess assets.

S&P acknowledged the additional weaknesses identified in its review but did not lower the score further because 5 is already the bottom of its assessment scale.

S&P Questions Tether’s Regulatory Oversight and Reserve Safeguards

The agency also raised concerns about the regulatory framework governing Tether in El Salvador, where the company relocated in January 2025.

The country’s National Commission of Digital Assets requires 70% of reserves to be held in assets that can be liquidated within 30 days. However, S&P described the framework as broad, allowing assets such as Bitcoin, gold and loans to qualify despite their higher risk profiles.

Another concern involves the absence of a requirement to segregate reserve assets from the issuer’s other holdings. S&P noted that regulators in the United States and Europe generally expect stronger safeguards in this area. Without publicly available information confirming asset segregation, the agency said it could not determine how effectively USDT’s reserves are protected from broader corporate risks.

Tether’s Audit Disclosure Remains a Point of Contention

In August 2026, KPMG issued an unqualified opinion on Tether’s 2025 accounts, which the company described as its first full independent audit. Tether presented the development as support for its financial reporting. However, S&P said the audited financial statements and auditor’s report had not been published, limiting its ability to independently examine the underlying information.

The agency also highlighted that Tether’s reserve reports do not identify the custodians and counterparties holding its assets. Its attestations are published quarterly, while some competing stablecoin issuers provide monthly updates. Tether has challenged S&P’s assessments before. Following the initial downgrade in 2025, CEO Paolo Ardoino criticized the agency on X, saying the company wore its criticism with pride and pointing to previous financial collapses as evidence of weaknesses in traditional systems.

Despite maintaining the lowest rating, S&P acknowledged that USDT had demonstrated a strong record of price stability, particularly over the previous 12 months.

Can Tether address S&P’s concerns by improving reserve disclosures and reducing exposure to higher-risk assets? Will USDT’s established record of price stability continue to outweigh concerns about its reserve structure as the stablecoin market matures?

title: Tether Pushes Back Against S&P as USDT Reserve Maintains Lowest Stability Assessment
description: Tether pushes back against S&P Global Ratings after the agency maintained its lowest stability assessment for USDT, pointing to a growing share of higher-risk assets in the stablecoin’s reserves and continuing concerns about transparency. In its latest assessment, published November 18, S&P kept USDT’s ability to maintain its dollar peg at 5 (weak), the lowest […]
fullContent:
Tether pushes back against S&P Global Ratings after the agency maintained its lowest stability assessment for USDT, pointing to a growing share of higher-risk assets in the stablecoin’s reserves and continuing concerns about transparency.

In its latest assessment, published November 18, S&P kept USDT’s ability to maintain its dollar peg at 5 (weak), the lowest score on its five-point scale. The rating remains unchanged from November 2025, when the agency first downgraded the stablecoin. Tether rejected the assessment, arguing that the problem lies with S&P’s evaluation framework rather than the composition of its reserves. The company also referenced The Big Short, the film about the 2008 financial crisis, in its response to the agency’s findings.

Higher-Risk Assets Account for 28% of USDT in Circulation

S&P’s latest concerns center on the changing composition of Tether’s reserves. According to the report, higher-risk holdings, including Bitcoin, gold, public equities, secured loans and corporate bonds, represented approximately 28% of USDT in circulation as of September 30.

That figure increased from 24% a year earlier, indicating a growing exposure to assets whose values can fluctuate with market conditions. S&P warned that a significant decline in the value of these holdings could leave USDT undercollateralized, particularly if several reserve assets experienced losses at the same time.

The company also argued that the agency’s own history demonstrated weaknesses in traditional financial risk assessments. Tether’s September 30 reserve report, attested by BDO, showed approximately $191.5 billion in assets against $183.5 billion in liabilities. This left the company with roughly $7.95 billion in excess assets.

S&P acknowledged the additional weaknesses identified in its review but did not lower the score further because 5 is already the bottom of its assessment scale.

S&P Questions Tether’s Regulatory Oversight and Reserve Safeguards

The agency also raised concerns about the regulatory framework governing Tether in El Salvador, where the company relocated in January 2025.

The country’s National Commission of Digital Assets requires 70% of reserves to be held in assets that can be liquidated within 30 days. However, S&P described the framework as broad, allowing assets such as Bitcoin, gold and loans to qualify despite their higher risk profiles.

Another concern involves the absence of a requirement to segregate reserve assets from the issuer’s other holdings. S&P noted that regulators in the United States and Europe generally expect stronger safeguards in this area. Without publicly available information confirming asset segregation, the agency said it could not determine how effectively USDT’s reserves are protected from broader corporate risks.

Tether’s Audit Disclosure Remains a Point of Contention

In August 2026, KPMG issued an unqualified opinion on Tether’s 2025 accounts, which the company described as its first full independent audit. Tether presented the development as support for its financial reporting. However, S&P said the audited financial statements and auditor’s report had not been published, limiting its ability to independently examine the underlying information.

The agency also highlighted that Tether’s reserve reports do not identify the custodians and counterparties holding its assets. Its attestations are published quarterly, while some competing stablecoin issuers provide monthly updates. Tether has challenged S&P’s assessments before. Following the initial downgrade in 2025, CEO Paolo Ardoino criticized the agency on X, saying the company wore its criticism with pride and pointing to previous financial collapses as evidence of weaknesses in traditional systems.

Despite maintaining the lowest rating, S&P acknowledged that USDT had demonstrated a strong record of price stability, particularly over the previous 12 months.

Can Tether address S&P’s concerns by improving reserve disclosures and reducing exposure to higher-risk assets? Will USDT’s established record of price stability continue to outweigh concerns about its reserve structure as the stablecoin market matures?

title: Bitcoin's DARKEST Hour Is Near (20 Days LEFT)
US Launches Crypto Crime Center With TRM Labs to Track Scams, Stolen Funds
description: The US launches Crypto Crime Center, a new initiative to disrupt criminal networks behind online scams, cybercrime, and cryptocurrency theft, bringing together federal investigators, state and local agencies, financial institutions, and technology companies. The newly established Threat Disruption Center aims to shorten the time between a victim reporting a crime and authorities taking action to […]
fullContent:
The US launches Crypto Crime Center, a new initiative to disrupt criminal networks behind online scams, cybercrime, and cryptocurrency theft, bringing together federal investigators, state and local agencies, financial institutions, and technology companies.

The newly established Threat Disruption Center aims to shorten the time between a victim reporting a crime and authorities taking action to trace and potentially freeze stolen funds. The initiative will involve more than 30 federal agencies and over 440 state and local partners. Blockchain analytics company TRM Labs has been selected to provide the center’s primary investigative technology under a federal contract worth $94.66 million.

The launch comes as cryptocurrency-related fraud continues to generate substantial losses. The FBI recorded more than $11 billion in reported losses involving cryptocurrency during 2025, highlighting the need for faster coordination between investigators and private-sector platforms.

Threat Disruption Center Brings Agencies and Crypto Platforms Together

The Threat Disruption Center will operate as a shared investigative resource, allowing law enforcement agencies to exchange information with participating companies as they identify victims, trace transactions and investigate criminal networks.

The approach is intended to help authorities intervene before scammers move stolen funds beyond recovery. Cryptocurrency exchanges and payment providers may be able to stop transfers or freeze assets, while social media companies can remove accounts used to contact and deceive victims.

Law enforcement agencies will continue conducting investigations and pursuing court-authorized asset seizures as part of the broader effort. John A. Condon, acting executive associate director of Homeland Security Investigations, said the partnerships would help authorities identify and dismantle criminal networks more quickly, disrupt fraud at its source and protect potential victims.

The center also reflects a broader effort to strengthen cooperation between government agencies and private companies as online fraud becomes increasingly organized across international borders.

According to the FBI’s 2025 Internet Crime Report, the bureau received 181,565 complaints involving cryptocurrency. Crypto investment fraud accounted for approximately $7.2 billion of the more than $11 billion in reported cryptocurrency-related losses. The FBI has also identified criminal networks operating in Southeast Asia among those responsible for many of these schemes. Some operations involve trafficked individuals who are forced to participate in fraudulent activities.

TRM Labs Secures $94.66 Million Contract for Investigative Technology

TRM Labs will provide Ardence as the Threat Disruption Center’s primary investigative platform. The technology will help investigators process victim complaints, trace cryptocurrency transactions and map the networks responsible for fraudulent activity.

Government procurement records show that TRM Labs received a $94.66 million contract in July to support the initiative. The agreement is scheduled to run through August 29, 2027. The company will supply the technology and investigative capabilities needed to support cooperation between participating agencies and private-sector partners.

By connecting transaction data with information about criminal networks, investigators aim to identify where stolen assets are moving and determine whether intervention is still possible. The platform is also intended to help authorities identify connections between separate complaints, potentially revealing larger operations that target multiple victims through similar methods.

FBI’s Operation Level Up Provides a Foundation for the Initiative

The Threat Disruption Center builds on existing government efforts to identify cryptocurrency fraud victims and prevent additional losses.

One example is Operation Level Up, an FBI initiative launched in 2024 to identify people targeted by cryptocurrency investment scams and warn them before they send additional money to criminals.

According to the bureau, the operation has notified more than 8,000 victims and helped prevent over $500 million in losses. The new center expands the scope of this approach by bringing more agencies and private-sector companies into a shared operational framework.

For the cryptocurrency industry, the development highlights the growing importance of cooperation between exchanges, analytics providers and law enforcement agencies. Faster information-sharing could help limit fraud-related losses, although the effectiveness of the new center will ultimately depend on how quickly participating organizations can act and how often stolen funds can actually be recovered.

Will the Threat Disruption Center significantly reduce cryptocurrency-related fraud by enabling faster intervention? Could closer cooperation between US authorities and crypto platforms lead to stronger expectations for exchanges and other digital asset service providers?

title: Hong Kong SFC Flags Hyperliquid as a Suspicious Trading Platform
description:
Hong Kong’s Securities and Futures Commission (SFC) has added Hyperliquid to its list of suspicious virtual asset trading platforms, saying the platform is not licensed to provide services in the city. 
This is not the first time a financial regulator has flagged Hyperliquid. In May, the UK Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) urged people to stay away from the platform, saying it "may be providing or promoting financial services or products without our permission". 
Onchain Architecture Does Not Offer Immunity
In its warning published on 18 November, the regulator said Hyperliquid may be actively marketing its services to local investors, but accounts and assets held through Hyperliquid are outside the supervision applied to SFC-licensed platforms. 
The regulator also warned that clients of unlicensed platforms could lose their holdings if an operator collapses, stops trading, is hacked, or misappropriates assets.  The notice covers Hyperliquid at the platform level, without separately addressing spot and perpetual products. 
 Hong Kong’s licensing rules apply to platforms operating in Hong Kong and to overseas companies that target  Hong Kong investors. Thus, offshore registration or an on-chain trading model does not automatically place a platform outside the local regulatory perimeter.
What Other Platforms Should Check 
When assessing financial platforms, regulators review more than just the legal address. They will look at whether the crypto platform, the broker, the wallet and the trading venue will allow onboarding, whether they will run local advertising and whether they will have a referral programme. 
Companies also need to look at the permissions by product. A licence to trade virtual assets doesn't necessarily cover derivative style contracts or all the associated services.
Under the HK Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Terrorist Financing Ordinance, it is a criminal offence to actively market unlicensed virtual asset services to the HK public. Such activity may lead to access blocking orders, banking restrictions and enforcement against the local promoter or affiliates.


This article was written by Tanya Chepkova at www.financemagnates.com.

title: XRP Exchange Balances Drop 190M to 5.11B, Lowest Since Oct 12
description:
CoinGlass shows XRP exchange balances fell about 190 million coins in eight days to 5.11 billion on November 19. That print is the lowest since October 12. Futures open interest sat near 1.95 billion XRP on the same window, while the XRP price sat around $0.98. Exchange wallets and futures desks have found themselves at […]
The post XRP Exchange Balances Drop 190M to 5.11B, Lowest Since Oct 12 appeared first on Live Bitcoin News.
fullContent:
CoinGlass shows XRP exchange balances fell about 190 million coins in eight days to 5.11 billion on November 19. That print is the lowest since October 12. Futures open interest sat near 1.95 billion XRP on the same window, while the XRP price sat around $0.98. Exchange wallets and futures desks have found themselves at opposing ends of the same tape. The drawdown is a symptom of coins leaving venue books while leveraged bets stay large.

XRP Exchange Balances Hit a Multi-Week Low

On November 11, CoinGlass put combined XRP exchange balances near 5.3 billion. By November 19 the same tracker showed about 5.11 billion. The gap is roughly 190 million XRP over eight sessions. That leaves the venue stock at its softest reading since October 12. Exchange balances measure coins parked on centralized venues, not the full circulating supply. A lower total means less XRP sits on those books for immediate sale.

CoinGlass tracks the stock across the exchanges it covers. The eight-day exit does not name which wallets moved the coins. It also does not prove those tokens went into long-term cold storage. It does show the venue side of the XRP market thinned while price stayed soft. That is the number that matters for anyone watching sellable float.

A thinner exchange book can cut the pool of coins ready to hit the order book on a down tape. It can also reflect withdrawals into private wallets, OTC desks, or other venues outside the tracker set. The CoinGlass series does not settle that split. It only shows that the covered exchange total fell by about 190 million XRP in eight days and landed at 5.11 billion.

Futures Open Interest Stays Near 1.95B XRP

Derivatives did not empty with the spot books. CoinGlass put XRP futures open interest near 1.95 billion XRP, about $1.91 billion in notional terms, on the same November 19 window. Earlier prints had left futures exposure closer to 2.36 billion XRP. Coin-denominated open interest also cooled, yet the book stayed heavy beside spot near $0.98.

Open interest counts outstanding contracts. It does not say whether those bets lean long or short. It also does not forecast the next print. It does say leveraged desks still held a large XRP position while exchange balances fell. That mix keeps liquidation risk and funding swings in play even when the spot float on venues is lighter.

The two series pull in different directions for a markets reader. Thinner exchange balances usually shrink the pool of coins ready for immediate sale. Large open interest keeps the leveraged side of the market alive. The clash is about where the coins sit, and the leveraged book remains in place.

Geneva, Switzerland, November 19, 2026 — Pulsar Money today announced support for USDT deposits on the TRON network, allowing users to fund their Pulsar accounts with USDT (TRC-20) and access everyday payment features through the app.

 

With this integration, users can deposit USDT on TRON and use their balances for online purchases, subscriptions, and other everyday expenses through the Pulsar virtual card. Pulsar charges no fees for supported stablecoin deposits across its plans, although network and third-party fees may apply.

 

The integration connects TRON’s widely adopted stablecoin infrastructure with Pulsar’s consumer-focused payment platform. In Q3 2026, TRON processed $2.21 trillion in stablecoin settlement volume, averaging $24 billion daily. “TRON’s extensive stablecoin activity reflects the growing demand for accessible, efficient digital payments,” said Sam Elfarra, Community Spokesperson for TRON DAO. “Pulsar’s integration brings that infrastructure closer to everyday use, expanding how people can access and spend their stablecoins.”

 

Pulsar combines stablecoin balance management and payment features in a single app. To deposit USDT on TRON, users can select the supported asset and network in the Pulsar app and follow the deposit instructions. Users should ensure they select TRON (TRC-20) and send only USDT to the deposit address provided for that network. Features and availability may vary by region and service provider.

Pulsar Money is a money app that brings stablecoins and everyday payment features together. Users can manage supported balances and access services including a virtual card and currency conversion, subject to availability and provider terms. Pulsar is not a bank.

description:
The question isn’t simply whether humanity should race toward superintelligence or stop. Nick Bostrom argues the harder challenge is preserving the ability to slow down when safety falls behind, without turning a temporary pause into permanent technological stagnation.
a16z’s Eddy Lazzarin and Elena Burger sit down with Bostrom to revisit the ideas he helped bring into the mainstream, now that increasingly capable AI systems actually exist. They discuss why alignment may become harder as models grow more situationally aware, which capability improvements may carry more risk than others, and why Bostrom favors “pacing the frontier” rather than committing to a broad or indefinite pause.
They also examine the cost of waiting. Bostrom argues that safely developed superintelligence could radically extend human lifespans and address problems from disease to poverty, meaning delay carries risks of its own. From there, the conversation turns to Deep Utopia, governance, the possibility of post-human forms of life, the simulation argument, and whether AI could eventually surpass humans at philosophy itself.

title: Chainlink Price Down 41% Since September: Is $9 the Floor?
description:
Key Takeaways LINK still holds support near $8.81 Four sessions of small candles, no follow-through 50-day average meets the 100-day […]
The post Chainlink Price Down 41% Since September: Is $9 the Floor? appeared first on Coindoo.
fullContent:
Key Takeaways

  • LINK still holds support near $8.81
  • Four sessions of small candles, no follow-through
  • 50-day average meets the 100-day
  • First resistance sits near $10.1–$10.30

When Coindoo last checked Chainlink on November 15, LINK had just bounced 4% after five red days, and the open question was whether that move marked a turn or a pause.

What Changed Since the November 15 Bounce

Four sessions later, the chart leans toward a pause. LINK has printed a row of small daily candles just above $9 and trades around $9.22 on the Binance daily chart, almost exactly where it stood on November 15.

Today’s session opened at $9.08, dipped to $8.97 and has climbed to $9.22, a 1.46% gain with more than nine hours of trading left. Buyers keep defending the $9 area, but they have not lifted the price far from it.

Trading activity has thinned out as well. The heavy red volume bar from the mid-November breakdown stands well above anything traded since, and today’s session has drawn about 597,000 LINK so far.

The session also brought news from traditional finance. UBS has used Chainlink to run key lifecycle steps for a tokenized structured note on Ethereum, in what the two firms describe as a production pilot for a market they put above $2 trillion in outstanding notional. For LINK holders, the connection is indirect: Chainlink’s standard company description refers to a model in which enterprise revenue is converted into LINK and held in the Chainlink Reserve, but the announcement does not tie the UBS pilot to that model. On the chart, the day’s modest gain keeps LINK inside the same narrow range.

The Floor Holding LINK Up

That floor is the 0.786 Fibonacci retracement near $8.81. This chart measures the retracement from the June wick low of $6.92 to the late-September peak at $15.76, which places the level slightly below the $8.89 used on November 15, when the swing low was set at $7.02.

So far, only wicks have broken it. The November 15 sell-off reached about $8.62 before buyers stepped in, and no daily candle has closed below $8.81 since. Many traders treat the 0.786 as the last retracement before a rally is given back almost entirely. For LINK, a close below it would bring the $7-$7.95 demand zone flagged last time, and the June low beneath it, back into view.

The Ceiling Keeps Dropping

The levels above price have also moved against LINK. It tested the overlap of its 200-day simple moving average at $10.1 and the 0.618 retracement near $10.30 in the first half of November, then lost both in the mid-November breakdown. That former floor is now the first resistance.

Higher up, the averages are sliding. The 50-day SMA, which stood at $12.09 on November 15, has fallen to $11.65 and now sits just under the 100-day SMA at $11.70 on the live candle, close to the 0.5 retracement around $11.34. A daily close at those readings would confirm that the shorter average has crossed beneath the longer one, a shift traders associate with medium-term weakness.

Momentum has not turned either. The 14-day RSI reads 34.61, slightly below its 35.12 signal line, after dipping toward oversold levels in mid-November.

How far each level sits from $9.22

100-day SMA · $11.70+26.9%
50-day SMA · $11.65+26.4%
0.5 Fib · around $11.34+23.0%
0.618 Fib · near $10.30+11.7%
200-day SMA · $10.1+9.7%
LINK now$9.22
0.786 Fib · near $8.81−4.4%
June swing low · $6.92−24.9%

Three Closes to Watch

Each scenario depends on where daily candles finish.

The base holds

Daily closes stay above $8.81 and RSI turns back above its 35.12 signal line. That combination would point to selling pressure fading at deep support and put the $10.1-$10.30 zone back within reach.

The trend is reclaimed

Daily closes back above $10.30 would undo the November breakdown and bring the $11.34-$11.70 cluster, formed by the 0.5 retracement and the 50- and 100-day SMAs, into play.

The floor gives way

A decisive daily close below $8.81 would remove the last nearby Fibonacci support and leave the June swing low at $6.92 as the next major reference on this chart.

A climb to $10.30, the best case above, would still win back only part of the November drop. LINK would remain below two of its three major averages, with the 0.5 level and the 50- and 100-day SMAs packed within about 40 cents of each other just overhead.

The technical levels and scenarios described reflect chart readings at the time of writing and are not predictions of future price movements. Cryptocurrency markets are highly volatile, and readers should do their own research and consider consulting a licensed financial adviser before making any investment decisions.

fullContent:
November 19th, 2026 – Grand Cayman, Cayman Islands

class=”ql-align-center”>Anchorage Digital, Fluid, HoneyB, and Upshift support institutional and retail access to Bitcoin on Sui with BitGo, Inc. expected to follow in 2027

Hashi, Sui’s native Bitcoin finance infrastructure, is now live on mainnet, with more than 20 custody, retail, and DeFi participants.

Bitcoin has spent years becoming one of the world’s largest pools of capital. Now the infrastructure to put it to work has arrived, forming one of the broadest coalitions in Bitcoin finance. 

That coalition is still growing fast. The latest to join Hashi are Merkl, an onchain incentive platform; and Current, a lending protocol. These additions expand the ecosystem of DeFi products and services being built around Bitcoin on Sui.

Bitcoin-Native Finance, Now Live

Hashi keeps Bitcoin on the Bitcoin network and mints hBTC, a 1:1 Bitcoin-backed asset, on Sui. That hBTC can then serve as collateral for lending, borrowing, and other onchain financial products. 

Hashi is decentralized by design. It’s secured by validators, not a single entity, using industry-leading cryptography. On top of that foundation, it connects leading providers across custody, trading, and decentralized finance to build financial products, giving Bitcoin holders many ways to put their assets to work.

Accessing Bitcoin Finance on Sui

With hBTC now live, Bitcoin holders have a new set of opportunities at their fingertips. That starts with borrowing against BTC and accessing new financial strategies through lending markets and vaults. 

To meet the specific needs of institutions, several new providers are offering new lending and vault facilities. 

Fluid’s institutional-grade lending protocol is now live on Sui, beginning with Bitcoin-backed stablecoin loans. Bitcoin holders can use Hashi to bring BTC onto Sui as hBTC, then use it as collateral on Fluid to borrow stablecoins, starting with USDC with more flows coming. 

“Bitcoin is the largest pool of idle capital in crypto,” said Samyak Jain, founder and CEO at Fluid. “With Hashi, it can now power deep, capital-efficient credit markets on Fluid.”

Institutional Access, Retail Opportunities, and Liquidity

For institutions, that infrastructure shows up as a custody problem solved. Institutions will be able to use both leading crypto custodians, Anchorage Digital and BitGo, Inc. (“BitGo”) to access Hashi. This model gives institutions a path to hold or deploy BTC into Hashi. Previously announced institutional partners, such as Cumberland and Wave Digital Assets will all play roles as early participants in deploying BTC and stablecoins on Hashi, providing liquidity to a variety of strategies on Sui. Sui DeFi protocols, including Blueprint Finance (Concrete), Bluefin, Cetus, Current, and Suilend will also unlock new lending opportunities, stablecoin credit, and yield strategies backed by Bitcoin. 

“Some of the world’s largest Bitcoin holders are sitting on enormous amounts of untapped financial potential,” said Nathan McCauley, CEO and Co-Founder at Anchorage Digital. “Hashi gives our institutional clients a new way to access Bitcoin finance on Sui, with their BTC held in custody at Anchorage Digital Bank.”

If you’re an institution interested in deploying BTC or stablecoins on Hashi, please reach out to your custodian or hashi@sui.io. Users can explore more at sui.io/hashi. 

About Sui

Sui, where money moves as freely as messages, is a next-generation Layer 1 blockchain built for agentic finance and scalable global payments. Founded by the core team behind Meta’s stablecoin initiative and powered by an object-centric model, Sui makes assets, permissions, and user data programmable and ownable. Sui’s primitives offer builders everything they need to create high-performance payments and financial applications, including instant agentic payments. Learn more at sui.io.

title: Hong Kong Regulator Flags Hyperliquid DEX as Suspicious, but HYPE Shrugs Off The Warning
description:

The post Hong Kong Regulator Flags Hyperliquid DEX as Suspicious, but HYPE Shrugs Off The Warning appeared first on 99Bitcoins.
fullContent:
Hong Kong’s Securities and Futures Commission (SFC) added Hyperliquid to its public alert list of suspicious virtual asset trading platforms on Wednesday, November 18. The listing, under the name “Hyperliquid / Hyperliquid Hong Kong,” marks the decentralized exchange as unlicensed in the city. For Hyperliquid, one of the largest decentralized exchanges for futures trading, it is a rare public warning from a major financial regulator. It also lands while HYPE is already 30% below its September high.

HYPE, Hyperliquid’s token, dipped about 4% after the listing but was back above its pre-listing price by Thursday, trading near $69. We compared its hourly moves with Bitcoin’s and checked whether money left the exchange. Both point the same way: so far, traders have treated this Hyperliquid news as noise.

So is the SFC alert a real threat to Hyperliquid, or just paperwork?

A Warning Without a Ban For Hyperliquid HYPE, At Least for Now

The SFC keeps an alert list of firms it says are not licensed in Hong Kong but are suspected of serving or marketing to people there. It is a warning to investors, not a ban or a lawsuit. The regulator says users of unlicensed platforms have no protection under its rules and could struggle to get money back if something goes wrong.

Hyperliquid works differently from most names on the list. It is a decentralized exchange: trades settle on its own blockchain, and users connect a crypto wallet instead of opening an account. That makes it harder for a regulator to shut down, but it also means Hong Kong users get none of the protections a licensed exchange must offer.

So far, the alert hasn’t come with more:

  • No block or suspension: no website block or trading suspension has been announced.
  • No reply yet: Hyperliquid had not publicly responded as of Thursday.

DISCOVER: Hyperliquid Jumps After Trump Regulatory Comments

To separate the Hong Kong effect from the wider market, we lined up hourly prices for HYPE and Bitcoin on Hyperliquid, starting at 12:00 UTC on November 18.

  • The dip: HYPE’s lowest hourly close was 4.0% below the starting point, late on Wednesday. Bitcoin was down 2.9% in the same hour.
  • The recovery: by midday Thursday, HYPE was 0.7% above where it started, while Bitcoin was still 0.3% lower.
  • Exchange deposits: the Hyperliquid bridge, where users park dollars to trade, held $5.70 billion on Thursday, up slightly from $5.68 billion on November 17. Deposits had fallen 8% in the week before the listing, but they stopped falling after it.

HYPE did drop a bit harder than Bitcoin, but most of the move matched the wider market. If Hong Kong traders were rushing for the exits, deposits would show it. They don’t, at least not yet.

DISCOVER: Next 1000X Crypto – Here’s 10+ Crypto Tokens That Can Hit 1000x This Year

A Busy List: 14 Trading Platforms Flagged This Year

We counted every entry the SFC has filed under suspicious trading platforms. Hyperliquid is the 14th this year and the 69th since 2021.

  • By year: 1 in 2021, 3 in 2022, 7 in 2023, 32 in 2024, 12 in 2025 and 14 so far in 2026.
  • Familiar names: MEXC was added in February 2024 and BTCC in October 2026.
  • The warning case: JPEX was flagged in July 2022. It collapsed the following year in one of Hong Kong’s largest crypto fraud cases.

Many of the other entries are little-known sites, including look-alikes of the licensed exchange HashKey. Hyperliquid stands out as one of the largest platforms on the list, with $6.3 billion of futures traded on it in the past 24 hours.

For HYPE, the bigger risk is what comes next. Other regulators could follow Hong Kong, and big exchanges that list HYPE may face questions from their own regulators. For now, this Hyperliquid news carries no sign of an immediate crackdown.

HYPE Price Analysis: Holding Near the 200-Day Average

On the daily chart, HYPE trades at $68.99. It is close to its 200-day exponential moving average (EMA), an average that gives recent prices more weight, at $69.44, and below its 50-day EMA at $77.64. The 14-day relative strength index (RSI), a 0-100 gauge of momentum, reads 39.6, below the neutral 50.

HYPE is still up 171% this year, from $25.45 on January 1, while Bitcoin is down 28%. But it has fallen about 30% from its September 23 high of $98.

  • Support: $58.3, where HYPE turned in June, July and August. Last Friday’s low of $59.70 came close to it.
  • Resistance: $75.5, a level that held as support in September and October and capped HYPE in June. Above that, $89, where HYPE turned in September and October.
Path What has to happen Next stop
Bullish A daily close above $75.5 $89, the September-October turning point
Sideways Price holds between $58.3 and $75.5 A range around the 200-day EMA
Bearish A daily close below $58.3 $51.5, the June and August lows

For Hyperliquid HYPE, the thing to watch is whether other regulators follow Hong Kong. If none do and bridge deposits keep holding above $5.6 billion, the SFC alert will likely fade from view. A second warning from a major market, or a drop in deposits, would be a clearer sign that traders are worried.

description:

fullContent:
Nvidia could be about to hand its biggest job to the man who helped turn Arm into one of the world’s most valuable chip companies. Rene Haas is now being considered as a potential successor to Jensen Huang at Nvidia, a familiar face at the center of the AI industry’s biggest leadership change.

Bloomberg reported that Nvidia’s recruitment firm had approached Haas as part of its search for a new chief executive. Haas previously spent seven years at Nvidia before joining Arm in 2013. He became Arm’s CEO in 2022 and has since overseen its expansion into the booming AI infrastructure market.

An appointment would put someone with experience at both companies in charge of Nvidia’s next chapter. But what does it mean for crypto? Could Haas push the AI boom even further, and what would that mean for Bitcoin and the rest of the market?

Rene Haas Turned Arm Into an AI Infrastructure Player, But Could He Do the Same at Nvidia?

Haas is not an outsider to Nvidia. He previously ran the company’s computing products business between 2006 and 2013, giving him direct experience with the company before its transformation into an AI powerhouse.

His subsequent run at Arm offers a glimpse of what he might bring to the role. Arm reported $4.92 billion in revenue for its fiscal 2026, up from $4.01 billion the previous year. Its profit before tax climbed from $756 million to $960 million. The company has also moved beyond its traditional chip-design licensing business, introducing its own AGI CPU for AI data centers in March 2026.

Arm’s technology already reaches more than 99% of smartphones sold worldwide. Its designs also power computing infrastructure used by major cloud providers and Nvidia itself.

Haas helped position the company for a much larger role in the AI economy. Now, his next challenge could be taking Nvidia beyond selling the chips powering that expansion.

Nvidia’s existing business gives him an enormous starting point. The company generated $115.8 billion in quarterly revenue in its latest results, with data center sales accounting for $107.6 billion. Revenue increased 103% from a year earlier.

Its next-generation Vera Rubin platform has also entered production and begun shipping. A new CEO would inherit an extraordinary growth engine, but also the responsibility of deciding how aggressively Nvidia should expand its influence across the AI industry.

If Haas brings his Arm strategy to Nvidia, we could see a push into integrated computing platforms, data center infrastructure and new AI applications. That could create another wave of investment across the technology sector.

Haas and Crypto: What Will Happen?

Crypto could benefit if Haas turns Nvidia’s next chapter into another catalyst for AI infrastructure spending. The connection extends beyond tokens carrying artificial intelligence branding. Bitcoin and Ethereum have increasingly moved in tandem with technology stocks during periods when investors shift between risk assets.

A stronger Nvidia could help restore confidence in the AI investment cycle, especially if investors believe its leadership transition will not interrupt infrastructure spending.

Decentralized computing projects such as Render, Bittensor, Artificial Superintelligence Alliance, and Akash could also benefit. These networks are trying to capture demand for GPU resources, distributed computing, and AI development.

More spending on AI infrastructure would create opportunities for decentralized alternatives. Developers need computing power, and centralized providers cannot always meet every requirement at the right price.

The bigger opportunity could come from investor appetite rather than immediate demand for crypto tokens. If Nvidia shares regain momentum under Rene Haas, technology investors could become more comfortable taking risks elsewhere. That would give crypto a potential source of buying interest.

Haas has already demonstrated what he can do with Arm. Taking over Nvidia would give him a considerably larger platform, with consequences extending well beyond semiconductor stocks.

title: Introducing Kraken TV: live crypto markets and news on the big screen
description:
Live prices, movers and news on your television, built to be read from across the room or up close.
The post Introducing Kraken TV: live crypto markets and news on the big screen appeared first on Kraken Blog.
fullContent:
TL;DR

  • Kraken TV is a new app for Apple TV, Android TV (including Google TV) and Amazon Fire TV that turns your television into a live crypto market screen. No account, no sign-in and no setup: install it and it works.
  • The new News experience offers a headline-first feed, a saved reading list and a scrolling Market Wire ticker, plus Small, Medium and Big layouts that adapt to how far you’re sitting from the screen, which you can change at any time.
  • An ambient screensaver keeps the latest prices, news and events for your chosen coins on screen for hours, without your TV going to sleep.
  • Kraken TV is a companion to the Kraken app: scan a QR code to continue on your phone and trade the coin there. No trading happens on the TV.

Crypto markets, now on the big screen

Crypto doesn’t stop moving, and your TV doesn’t have to either. Today we’re introducing Kraken TV, a new app for Apple TV, Android TV and Amazon Fire TV that turns your television into a live crypto market screen. Prices, movers and news are all designed to be read from across the room or up close.

There’s nothing to set up. Install Kraken TV and it works, with no account and no sign-in.

Live markets at a glance

Kraken TV opens on Markets, with live prices, 24-hour change and sparklines for the assets you care about, plus the biggest movers so you can see what’s heating up.

A built-in asset picker lets you choose which assets to prioritize, and your selection follows you across the app.

News you can read from the couch

News is the newest part of Kraken TV, and it’s the reason for this launch. We built a browsable, headline-first feed that’s easy to read from the couch:

  • Filter your feed by category or by asset to focus on what matters to you.
  • Open any story to read the full article on screen.
  • Star a story while you’re reading and it lands in your saved reading list.
  • Follow the Market Wire, a scrolling ticker that runs along the bottom of the screen.
  • Scan the QR code on a story that catches your eye to continue on your phone and trade that coin in the Kraken app.

Coin pages built around the news

Select any asset from the grid and you’ll land on its own coin page, built around that coin’s news. It’s a quick way to see what’s driving an asset without leaving the couch.

A screensaver that keeps the market in view

Kraken TV doubles as an ambient screensaver. Build your list of coins, and it keeps their latest prices, news and events on screen for hours without your TV going to sleep.

You stay in the loop without staring at the screen or hunting for information, which makes it a natural fit for a waiting area, a shared space or simply some background atmosphere.

Big, Small, and Medium: one app, three ways to read

The first time you open Kraken TV, we ask how far away you’re sitting. The app then lays itself out for that distance, and you can change your choice at any time:

  • Big uses bigger type and fewer rows, so everything stays legible from across the room.
  • Small shows denser detail for when you’re sitting close.
  • Medium sits in between.

Same app, three genuinely different reading experiences.

Built for a remote control

Kraken TV is designed for a remote, not a cursor. A left-hand rail gives you quick access to every surface, and each one opens as its own window, titled in the header so you always know where you are.

A companion to the Kraken app

Kraken TV is a companion to the Kraken app, not a replacement for it. When something on screen is worth acting on, like a story about a coin you follow, scan the QR code to continue in the Kraken app on your phone and trade from there. No trading happens on the TV.

Available on Apple TV, Android TV and Amazon Fire TV

One build covers Apple TV, Android TV (including Google TV) and Amazon Fire TV. Kraken TV is our first app on the Amazon Appstore. Download Kraken TV on your streaming device, pick how far away you’re sitting, and put the market on the big screen:

  • Apple TV (App Store)
  • Google TV/Android TV (Google Play)
  • Fire TV (Amazon Appstore)

The post Introducing Kraken TV: live crypto markets and news on the big screen appeared first on Kraken Blog.
