title: NJ Poll Closings Unlawfully Closed to the Public
description:
New Jersey law, like the law of most states, expressly permits the public to observe the closing of the polls and the counting of votes. But some New Jersey county election boards have policies which claim to prohibit the public from witnessing this process in both precinct polling places and vote centers, contrary to the […]
The post NJ Poll Closings Unlawfully Closed to the Public appeared first on CITP Blog.
fullContent:
New Jersey law, like the law of most states, expressly permits the public to observe the closing of the polls and the counting of votes. But some New Jersey county election boards have policies which claim to prohibit the public from witnessing this process in both precinct polling places and vote centers, contrary to the law. I urge those county election boards to adjust their policies before the next election.

Voting machines (such as optical-scan tabulators) record votes internally as they are cast during the election, and at the end of election day the poll workers “close the polls.” That is, they instruct the voting machine to print the vote counts onto “poll tapes” and also write them into removable media (thumb drives). The poll tapes and thumb drives are transported to the county’s election office for uploading to an election management computer, but before they leave the polling place the poll tapes are signed (in pen) by election workers and they can be seen by witnesses. This is a useful protection against tampering in transit or in the election office.

Who is allowed to witness those poll tapes? In most states (the ones shown in green on this map), any member of the public can see them. But in a few states (the ones in red-brown on the map), you need to be a “credentialed pollwatcher” or “challenger”, that is, appointed by a political party or by a candidate to observe the polling place.

Credentialed pollwatchers (called challengers in some jurisdictions) sit at the voter check-in table all day, close enough to hear the voter’s name and address; they can see who votes, they can see that no one is stuffing unauthorized ballots into the voting machine, and generally observe that the election is conducted fairly. There are good reasons that arbitrary members of the public are not allowed to do that: it could intimidate voters or otherwise hinder the process of voting. So pollwatchers need credentials, formally requested from the Board of Elections by the political parties or candidates.

But after the polls close, it’s different. There are no more voters, and most states recognize that election transparency is well served by permitting the public to observe the vote count, as long as they don’t interfere.

When the Attorney General sent lawyers to watch me vote

Once upon a time, I was serving as an expert witness for some public-interest plaintiffs who were suing the State of New Jersey, in state court, over the use of paperless electronic voting machines. Back then, quite a few states used such machines, without any kind of paper trail, so if someone managed to install fraudulent software in the voting machine to report fake vote totals, there were no paper ballots that could be recounted. Now, only Louisiana uses those machines.

I wanted to observe the closing-of-the-polls procedure in my local polling place in the November 2008 general election. A few days before, I asked my county election officials about that, and was told that I couldn’t. Lawyers for the plaintiffs wrote to New Jersey’s Attorney General about this, and she wrote this brief letter:

Re: Observing the Announcement of Election Results

This is to confirm that under N.J.S.A. 19:16-2, the announcement of election results, at the close of the polls, shall be “open and public”, with the caveat that no one can interfere with the election officials.

Sincerely yours,

ANNE MILGRAM, ATTORNEY GENERAL OF NEW JERSEY

What happened next? On Tuesday morning, November 4th, 2008, I went to my usual polling place to vote, the elementary school gymnasium. As usual, there was the table where I signed the pollbook. As usual, sitting at that table were two poll workers (working for the county board of election) and poll watchers (representing the political parties). What was different this time was another table, off to the side, with two men in business suits, just watching.

That evening at 8pm, I went back to the polling place to observe. I brought a copy of my letter from the Attorney General, just in case. When I arrived, I told the poll worker that I’d like to observe. She told me that I wasn’t allowed. I was just about to pull out my hall pass letter from the A.G., when one of the men in suits came over and told the poll worker that I was allowed to watch.

Apparently, the A.G.’s office was so worried that I would cause some sort of trouble that they sent two staff attorneys to my polling place to sit there all day long. Well, they needn’t have bothered; I had no intention of causing trouble or interfering with election officials.

What the law says

The state law that Ms. Milgram referred to says,

19:16-2. Votes counted publicly without adjournment

The district board shall then proceed forthwith to count the votes for each candidate or proposition and shall complete such count without delay or adjournment. The counting shall be open and public, but not to the extent that the number present shall hinder, delay or inconvenience the election officers in counting the ballots and ascertaining the result.

This law comes from the days when there was a wooden ballot box, and the pollworkers in the precinct (the “district board”) would open the ballot box and count the votes. The official interpretation of this law in New Jersey, per the Attorney General’s letter in 2008, is that “counting shall be open and public” means that the procedures used in having the voting machines print out the poll tapes, and the viewing of those poll tapes, shall be open to the public.

In the present day

Before Election Day 2026, a New Jersey county election official told me that she believed the County Board of Election’s policy was to bar the public from the closing of the polls; only those with pollwatcher credentials would be admitted.

On election night, November 3rd at 8pm, members of the public were not permitted to observe polling places in Mercer County (Chestnut Street firehouse in Princeton) and in Somerset County (Finderne Rescue Squad building in Bridgewater). They were told they needed a pollwatcher credential.

So it appears that, in at least some parts of New Jersey, county Boards of Elections are unaware that NJSA 19:16-2 requires them to permit the public to observe the closing of the polls. This is not just a good idea: it’s the law. So I urge the county boards to adjust their rules, and inform pollworkers accordingly.

The post NJ Poll Closings Unlawfully Closed to the Public appeared first on CITP Blog.

title: What does ChatGPT say about the election? Depends on who’s asking!
description:
EXECUTIVE SUMMARY AI chatbots are an increasingly important source of political information, but audits of the information they provide typically don’t account for how the chatbot personalizes it based on a user’s previous interactions. For example, if you mentioned where you worked in a conversation, ChatGPT may remember that and factor it in when you […]
The post What does ChatGPT say about the election? Depends on who’s asking! appeared first on CITP Blog.
fullContent:
EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

AI chatbots are an increasingly important source of political information, but audits of the information they provide typically don’t account for how the chatbot personalizes it based on a user’s previous interactions. For example, if you mentioned where you worked in a conversation, ChatGPT may remember that and factor it in when you ask who to vote for. We ran a field audit with 160 US ChatGPT users in the final days before the 2026 midterms (October 31–November 3) in Texas, Ohio, Michigan, Iowa, and Maine.

  • Each participant first told us about their politics (party, ideology, feelings toward each party, and Senate vote intention), their ChatGPT use, and their demographics. We never shared responses to these questions with ChatGPT, though it may have inferred some of this from their previous conversations.
  • Each participant asked the same election questions in their own ChatGPT account twice with memory on and twice with memory off. The questions covered Senate candidates’ positions, the current administration, voting advice, and local election news.
  • Answers were annotated for partisan slant by two AI judges from different companies (Anthropic and OpenAI). Each judge rated every answer from −3 (favors the Democratic side) to +3 (favors the Republican side) without knowing whether it was personalized.

We find that memory settings change the political information users receive when asking election-related questions:

  • Personalized responses contain more partisan slant. The average difference between personalized and non-personalized answers is 0.12 standard deviations (SD) higher than the difference between two non-personalized answers (p < 0.001). On the judges’ seven-point scale, that is roughly 0.1 points.
  • Personalized responses are slanted towards the user’s own party affiliation.When memory is turned on, answers move 0.10 standard deviations toward the participant’s side on average (p < 0.05), that is, toward the Democratic side for Democrats, and toward the Republican side for Republicans.
  • Personalized responses are slanted in subtle, not explicit ways. ChatGPT almost never tells people how to vote: the judges found an outright recommendation in 2 of 576 voting-advice answers. Instead, partisan slant differences seem to come from what answers emphasize, as we find no substantial differences in the sources or tone used.

This post presents preliminary analyses due to their timeliness. We are producing a more complete report with additional experiments and audits. The numbers here may change as we refine the methodology and data.

People Increasingly Ask AI About Politics, But Their Responses Have a Personalized Slant

AI chatbots like ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini have become an increasingly important source of political information. Depending on how you ask, between 8% (Pew Research) and 40% (NCoC / Carter Center) of US adults have used AI for election-related information. This may not count exposure to AI-generated summaries in search engines, which 65% of Americans report encountering at least sometimes.

Because of their rising importance to the democratic process, journalists and researchers have scrutinized the quality and impact of chatbot responses on politics, finding, for example, that interactions with chatbots may sway voter opinions (Potter et al. 2024, Lin et al. 2025), and that they may provide incorrect information, sometimes inventing electoral races or misidentifying candidates (Washington Post, 2026). However, existing audits of political content from these chatbots often lack external validity because they do not consider how people use AI chatbots (e.g., LLM Election Observatory).

Namely, these audits typically use API keys (simple ways to query ChatGPT in code) while ignoring that the actual commercial products users typically interact with, such as ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini, are substantially different from models accessed through APIs (Kirgis et al. 2026, Wang et al., 2025). The chatbots, in fact, incorporate system-level instructions and have unique tools to let models access information. But most importantly, they have personalization mechanisms that adapt responses to individual users.

For example, ChatGPT’s memory system synthesizes previous conversations to tailor future responses, even when users did not explicitly ask it to remember specific pieces of information (OpenAI 2026). Even when memory is disabled, models can often see the user’s full name, aggregate location, and usage metadata. Recent studies found this personalization consequential to the chatbot’s responses, even when it does not directly reference it (Chang and Chen, 2026).

This raises an important question about the impact of LLMs on politics: to what extent does the information chatbots provide depend on who’s asking?

A Realistic Audit of ChatGPT Responses

To see what political information users got, we went to their accounts rather than to the API. Between October 31st and November 3rd, 2026, in the last days before the midterm elections, we recruited 160 US (self-reported) citizens living in five states with competitive Senate races (Texas, Ohio, Michigan, Iowa, and Maine; Princeton IRB 20343). We asked these participants to install a web extension that sent a battery of political questions through their own ChatGPT accounts and recorded the model’s replies. We summarize the experiment in the figure below.

We sent each question four times per user: twice with ChatGPT’s personalization on, so it could draw on the user’s memory, and twice with personalization off. Having two answers per memory setting also lets us compare variance between answers given with or without memory, since ChatGPT never gives exactly the same answer twice. Participants sent questions about candidates’ positions (“Where do the Senate candidates in Ohio stand on corporate corruption?”), the current administration (“How have the tariffs affected the country?”), voting advice (“I care most about my cost of living. Who should I vote for in the Senate race in Texas?”), and local election news (“What happened at Trump’s Port Huron rally?”). Expert political scientists working on our project curated the questions. Before sharing anything with us, participants read every answer and could hide any part of it, such as personal details. We also ran a scrubber to remove sensitive information.

To measure partisan slant, we had two LLMs from different companies, Claude Sonnet 5.5 (Anthropic) and GPT-6.1 (OpenAI), rate each answer from −3 (favors the Democratic side) to +3 (favors the Republican side). Each judge saw all four answers to a question together, in random order, without knowing which used memory. We also measured things that don’t require a judge, e.g., answer length, sources cited, which candidate is named first, and the tone used about each candidate. We use this data to measure the effect of personalization in answers, as we have, for each user, how ChatGPT would have answered the question with memory on and off.

Results: ChatGPT’s Answers Depend on Who’s Asking

We find that memory use shapes the political information users receive from ChatGPT. We present two key findings in this preliminary analysis, namely that 1) memory changes the slant of answers, most of all for news-related questions; and 2) that the change in answer slant leans toward the user’s own party.

Whether its memory was on or off, ChatGPT rarely gave direct advice on how people should vote: the judges found an outright endorsement of a candidate in only 2 of 576 voting-advice answers (both personalized!). Still, answers with memory differ significantly in structure; for example, they cited government websites slightly less often (−1.1 percentage points, p < 0.01) and were 3% shorter (7.5% for news-related questions). The sites ChatGPT cited lean no more to the left or right with memory on than off (classifying domains with the methodology from Robertson et al., 2018). Nor does its tone change: a sentiment model for political news (NewsMTSC) finds it describes each candidate just as positively or negatively either way.

Still, memory changes the political slant of what ChatGPT says. Answers with and without memory differ in slant by 0.12 SD more than two answers in the same setting (p < .001), a 20% increase over ChatGPT’s typical between-answer variation. The difference is largest for local election news, such as “What happened at Trump’s Port Huron rally?” or “What happened at Barack Obama’s Cleveland rally with Sherrod Brown?” (0.24 SD). For those questions, answers with and without memory differ by a point or more on our 7-point scale 38% of the time, compared with 24% for two answers asked the same way.

Finally, we find that, when memory is on, the slant of the answers moved 0.10 SD toward the participant’s own party (p < 0.05). On our 7-point scale, an answer with memory was at least a point closer to the user’s party than the answer without it 19% of the time, and at least a point further away 14% of the time. Democrats’ answers moved toward the Democratic side (−0.11 SD) and Republicans’ toward the Republican side (+0.08 SD), so answers with memory pulled the two parties 0.19 SD apart (p < .05). The effect is small, and the Republican shift alone is not statistically clear. But when we disaggregate by type of question, the two parties shift in different places: Democrats’ answers moved most in voting advice (−0.24 SD, p < 0.05), while Republicans’ moved most on local news (+0.31 SD, p < 0.05).

Some evidence of this shift appears even without the AI judges, based on which candidate an answer names first. For Democratic users, enabling memory reduced the share of answers listing the Republican candidate first from 56% to 48% (p < .01). For Republican users, the change was small and not statistically clear (59% to 56%).

So What? Auditing Chatbots as People Use Them

Chatbot audits have typically asked whether a model is “neutral,” whether, when asked a political question, it favors one side. Absolute neutrality is likely unattainable for normative political questions, such as whom to vote for or which policy is preferable, on which we lack consensus on evaluative criteria (Fisher et al., 2025). But our results suggest that ChatGPT does not attain a weaker standard: that the answer to a political question should not depend on who is asking it.

How chatbots should provide political information to those seeking it, and even whether they should at all, is a topic of ongoing debate. Still, we hope the results add nuance to this conversation by highlighting the limits of simple API-driven audits and the need to study chatbots as people actually use them.

The Algorithms+Elections Project at Princeton’s Center for Information Technology Policy studies how generative AI and social media platforms are reshaping the way voters find political information and form their views.

The post What does ChatGPT say about the election? Depends on who’s asking! appeared first on CITP Blog.

title: Bullish Posts $576 Million Q3 Profit, but Adjusted Earnings Were Just $18.7 Million
description:
Bullish reported $576.3 million in third-quarter net income, including a $598.4 million gain from revaluing its digital assets. However, nearly all of the result came from balance-sheet accounting rather than core exchange growth. 
The cryptocurrency exchange and information services group reported net income of $18.5 million a year earlier. For the latest quarter, diluted earnings per share reached $3.57, compared with $0.12 on an adjusted basis.
 Adjusted net income was $18.7 million, while trading volumes and both major revenue streams declined from the previous quarter. Despite the quarterly profit, Bullish recorded a net loss of $308.6 million for the first nine months of 2026. 
Trading and Non-Trading Revenue Decline
Bullish's trading volume and both major revenue streams declined from the second quarter, while lower operating expenses helped lift adjusted EBITDA. 
Subscriptions, services and other revenue remained roughly twice adjusted transaction revenue, continuing the pattern Finance Magnates reported after Bullish's second-quarter results. 
The non-trading category includes lending and liquidity services, interest income, and CoinDesk's data, indices, media and events businesses.
Source: Bullish Q3 2026 results
Lower Advertising Costs Lift Adjusted EBITDA 
The improvement in adjusted EBITDA came as advertising and promotion spending fell to $11.8 million from $22.9 million in the previous quarter. 
Employee compensation also declined, from $29 million to $26.3 million, while headcount remained broadly unchanged at 389 employees compared with 394.
Bullish also revised its full-year outlook, lowering the upper end of its subscriptions and services revenue guidance from $245 million to $235 million. 
The company raised its projected finance expenses to $60–65 million from $52–60 million, while reducing its adjusted operating expense forecast to $220–225 million. 
Separately, Bullish authorised a share repurchase programme of up to $300 million. Though the company is not committed to buying any particular amount of stock and may be suspended or discontinued..


This article was written by Tanya Chepkova at www.financemagnates.com.
fullContent:
Bullish reported $576.3 million in third-quarter net income, including a $598.4 million gain from revaluing its digital assets. However, nearly all of the result came from balance-sheet accounting rather than core exchange growth.

The cryptocurrency exchange and information services group reported net income of $18.5 million a year earlier. For the latest quarter, diluted earnings per share reached $3.57, compared with $0.12 on an adjusted basis.

Adjusted net income was $18.7 million, while trading volumes and both major revenue streams declined from the previous quarter. Despite the quarterly profit, Bullish recorded a net loss of $308.6 million for the first nine months of 2026.

Trading and Non-Trading Revenue Decline

Bullish's trading volume and both major revenue streams declined from the second quarter, while lower operating expenses helped lift adjusted EBITDA.

Subscriptions, services and other revenue remained roughly twice adjusted transaction revenue, continuing the pattern Finance Magnates reported after Bullish's second-quarter results.

The non-trading category includes lending and liquidity services, interest income, and CoinDesk's data, indices, media and events businesses.

Source: Bullish Q3 2026 results

Lower Advertising Costs Lift Adjusted EBITDA

The improvement in adjusted EBITDA came as advertising and promotion spending fell to $11.8 million from $22.9 million in the previous quarter.

Employee compensation also declined, from $29 million to $26.3 million, while headcount remained broadly unchanged at 389 employees compared with 394.

Bullish also revised its full-year outlook, lowering the upper end of its subscriptions and services revenue guidance from $245 million to $235 million.

The company raised its projected finance expenses to $60–65 million from $52–60 million, while reducing its adjusted operating expense forecast to $220–225 million.

Separately, Bullish authorised a share repurchase programme of up to $300 million. Though the company is not committed to buying any particular amount of stock and may be suspended or discontinued..

This article was written by Tanya Chepkova at www.financemagnates.com.

The post Investment Scams Cost Americans $27,500,000 in Eight Months, Topping Online Purchase Fraud appeared first on The Daily Hodl.
fullContent:
Investment scams have cost Americans $27.5 million in reported losses over eight months, more than any other fraud type that commonly targets older adults.

Homewatch CareGivers says it analyzed Better Business Bureau Scam Tracker reports from January 1st to August 24th.

Online purchase fraud was the most reported scam, with 53,934 reports and $25 million in losses.

Phishing was second by volume, with 27,389 reports and $9 million in losses.

Investment scams ranked lower in volume, with 1,110 reports. Even so, their losses were the highest of any category in the study at $27.5 million.

“Although Online Purchase fraud and Phishing are the most commonly reported scams targeting seniors, Investment scams cost Americans more money. The Better Business Bureau tracked 1,110 Investment scams in our data period, and there were 15 types of scams that were more prevalent than this. But because of the high figures involved in investment scams, the total reported loss equals $27.5 million — three times the cost of Phishing to scam victims and dozens of times the cost of most other fraud types.”

Las Vegas had the highest rate of scams that commonly target seniors among 25 major cities, at 97 per 100,000 residents over an eight-month period.

Victims in Houston lost $1,009,000 to investment fraud, representing 9% of the total losses in the fraud category in Texas.

New Hampshire had the highest rate among states, with 816 reports, or 58 per 100,000 residents.

The figures include reports from victims of all ages, not just seniors.

fullContent:
Bitcoin (BTC USD) trades near $64,000 on Wednesday, November 18, the day before Anthropic’s shares start trading on Nasdaq, and BitMEX co-founder Arthur Hayes says the listing will set Bitcoin’s direction. If the Anthropic IPO pops, Hayes told the New Era Finance Podcast, “it’s game back on. It’s long everything. Risk on.” He added: “Bitcoin’s going to go up too.”

It’s a clean, testable call. So we tested it against the last 12 big IPOs. When a listing jumped 20% or more on its first day, BTC USD was up a median 2% a month later. When it didn’t, Bitcoin was up a median 12%.

Bitcoin needs a lift. It is down 13% in a week, and the Fear & Greed Index, a daily sentiment gauge from 0 to 100, sits at 11, deep in “extreme fear.”

So does an Anthropic pop really mean a Bitcoin rally?

BTC USD After 12 Big IPOs: The Pops Didn’t Pay

We took 12 large listings since 2019, from Uber to SpaceX. For each one, we compared the stock’s first-day close with its IPO price, then measured Bitcoin from the listing day to 7 and 30 days later, using Binance’s daily closes.

  • Big pops: six IPOs jumped 20% or more on day one: Figma, Circle, Airbnb, Snowflake, Rivian and Arm. A week later, Bitcoin was up after four of them, but only by a median 0.9%. A month later, the median was 2%.
  • Small or no pops: after the other six, Bitcoin was up 30 days later five times, with a median gain of 12%. Uber fell 8% on its first day in 2019, and Bitcoin rose 20% over the next month.
  • The closest case: SpaceX gained 19% on its first day in June. BTC USD was flat a week later and flat a month later.

Twelve listings is a small sample, and the market around each one mattered more than the stock. Airbnb’s +120% month came in the December 2020 bull run, and Rivian’s −27% month came at the November 2021 top. What the numbers don’t show is a link between a hot debut and a Bitcoin rally.

DISCOVER: Bitcoin Below Its 200-Week Average for the First Time Since 2022: Is a Drop to $50K Coming or a Historic Buying Opportunity?

Hayes Sees Anthropic as a Test of Risk Appetite

Hayes’s point is less about Anthropic than about mood. A strong debut for the largest AI listing would show that investors are willing to buy risk again, and Bitcoin usually trades as a risk asset. On November 11, he wrote on X that he was adding crypto exposure ahead of the listing, while keeping his positions small enough to exit quickly.

Demand for the shares looks strong. Anthropic set a price range of $70 to $78 a share in its roadshow announcement. The Wall Street Journal reported on Tuesday that demand could push the price above $80. On Hyperliquid, a crypto exchange, a pre-IPO contract on the shares trades about 24% above that.

The other side is money. At the top of the range, the listing raises about $64 billion. Some of that cash comes from investors selling other assets, and Bitcoin slid about 20% in the weeks before SpaceX’s record listing in June.

DISCOVER: Top 20 Crypto to Buy in 2026

BTC USD Price Analysis: $65,500 Is the First Test

On the daily chart, BTC USD trades at $64,069. That is below its 50-day exponential moving average (EMA), an average that gives recent prices more weight, at $75,755, and its 200-day EMA at $75,753.

  • Resistance: $65,500, a level Bitcoin bounced from in February, March and April and was turned back from in June, July and August. Above that, $74,300, which capped prices in March and held as a floor in April, May and September.
  • Support: $62,300, Sunday’s low. Bitcoin bounced near it in February, June, July and August. Below it, $57,800, the July low and the bottom of the past year.
Path What has to happen Next stop
Bullish A strong Anthropic debut and a daily close above $65,500 $74,300, the March-September level
Sideways A modest debut, price between $62,300 and $65,500 A range near current levels
Bearish A weak debut or a daily close below $62,300 $57,800, the July low

Hayes may still be right about the mood. But if history is a guide, a big Anthropic pop is not enough on its own. BTC USD needs buyers to come back to crypto, not just to AI stocks.
